title: Money, banks & payments
blurb: What money is, how banks really make money, who provides financial services, how deposits are protected and how payments move.

subs.title: What money is and the forms it takes
what: Money is anything people widely accept in exchange for goods and services. It does three jobs: a medium of exchange (you trade it instead of bartering), a unit of account or measure of value (prices are stated in it, so you can compare a $4 latte to a $40 shirt), and a store of value (you can hold it and spend it later). Inflation weakens the third job, which is why advisors say cash is for safety, not growth.

Today's U.S. dollar is fiat money: it has value because the government declares it legal tender and people trust it, not because it can be swapped for gold. Physical currency is a small share of the money supply. Most money is just bank-account balances that move electronically, which is why forms of exchange like debit cards, ACH transfers and mobile payments matter more every year.
how: Good money is durable, portable, divisible, uniform, limited in supply and widely accepted.
Currency types: coins (U.S. Mint), paper Federal Reserve notes (printed by the Bureau of Engraving and Printing), and government IOUs like Treasury bills, notes and bonds.

Forms of exchange: cash, checks, debit cards (money leaves your account now), credit cards (you borrow and pay later), electronic funds transfers such as ACH and wires, mobile wallets and peer-to-peer apps.
Barter fails because it needs a 'double coincidence of wants': both sides must want exactly what the other has.
Cryptocurrency works as a medium of exchange for some, but its price swings make it a weak unit of account and store of value.
nums: Cash was used for about 14% of U.S. consumer payments in 2024, down from about 31% in 2016 (Federal Reserve Diary of Consumer Payment Choice).
The U.S. Mint struck its last pennies for circulation in November 2025; each one cost about 3.7 cents to make (U.S. Treasury and U.S. Mint).
The U.S. ended the domestic gold standard in 1933 and ended gold convertibility for foreign governments in 1971 (Federal Reserve History).
real: A 2025 executive order directed federal agencies to phase out paper checks for most federal payments starting September 30, 2025, moving benefits and refunds to direct deposit and other electronic payments (U.S. Treasury).
Venezuela and Zimbabwe show what happens when a currency loses its store-of-value job: hyperinflation pushed people to use U.S. dollars instead.
traps: Debit is your money; credit is borrowed money. Exams often swap them.
A Treasury bond is a form of currency in the DECA PI list's sense (a government IOU), even though you can't spend it at a store.
subs.say: "Money has three jobs: to spend, to price things and to store value. Cash in a checking account does the first two well but loses ground on the third every year inflation runs above zero."

qs.q: Why shouldn't our client keep all of their savings in cash?
qs.a: Because cash is great for safety but poor at storing value over time. With inflation at about 3.7% in September 2026, $10,000 in a 0% account buys roughly $370 less a year later. We'd keep three to six months of expenses in an insured high-yield savings account for emergencies and invest money for goals five or more years away, so it can outgrow inflation. That way the client is safe now and still building wealth.

qs.q: Is cryptocurrency real money?
qs.a: It does some of money's jobs, but not all of them well. People can use it to pay, so it's a medium of exchange, but its price can swing 10% in a day, so it fails as a stable unit of account or store of value. Bitcoin fell about 64% in 2022, for example. If a client wants exposure, we'd cap it at a small slice they can afford to lose and keep their emergency fund in FDIC-insured dollars.

subs.title: How banks make money and how the Fed fits in
what: A bank is a middleman between savers and borrowers. It pays depositors interest, lends that money out at a higher rate, and keeps the difference, called the net interest margin. Banks also earn fee income from things like overdrafts, wire transfers, card interchange, wealth management and loan origination. A deposit is a liability for the bank (it owes you the money), and a loan is an asset (the borrower owes the bank).

Because banks lend out most deposits, they hold only a fraction in cash and reserves. This fractional-reserve system creates money: when a bank lends, the borrower's new account balance is new money in the economy. It also makes banks vulnerable to runs, which is why we have deposit insurance, capital rules and the Federal Reserve as lender of last resort. The Fed is the central bank: a Board of Governors in Washington, 12 regional Reserve Banks and the Federal Open Market Committee, which sets interest-rate policy.
how: Financial institutions perform intermediation: they pool savings, judge borrowers' credit, spread risk and make money liquid.
Banks are chartered by the federal government (supervised by the OCC) or a state, and are also overseen by the Fed and the FDIC.
Capital (the owners' money) absorbs losses before depositors do; regulators require minimum capital ratios under the Basel III framework.
The Fed's tools: the interest rate it pays on banks' reserves, open market operations (buying and selling Treasuries), and the discount window, where banks borrow in an emergency.
Reserve requirements have been 0% since March 2020, so today the Fed steers rates with interest on reserves rather than required reserves.
nums: There were 4,238 FDIC-insured institutions in the second quarter of 2026, down from more than 17,000 in 1984 (FDIC Quarterly Banking Profile and historical statistics).
U.S. banks earned $90.1 billion in net income in the second quarter of 2026 (FDIC Quarterly Banking Profile).
The prime rate is set at the top of the Fed's target range plus 3 points, so with the Fed at 3.75%-4.00% (Oct. 2026), prime is 7.00%.
real: Silicon Valley Bank failed in March 2023 after depositors pulled $42 billion in a single day; it had invested heavily in long-term bonds that lost value when rates rose (Federal Reserve review of SVB).
In 2008 the Fed lent hundreds of billions to banks and markets as lender of last resort, and Congress passed the $700 billion TARP program (Federal Reserve History).
traps: A deposit is the bank's liability, not its asset.
The Fed doesn't set your mortgage rate directly; it sets a short-term target that ripples out to other rates.
subs.say: "Your deposit doesn't sit in a vault. The bank lends it out and earns the spread, which is why it can pay you interest, and why the FDIC insures you up to $250,000 if something goes wrong."

qs.q: How does a bank actually make money off our deposits?
qs.a: Mostly from the spread. It pays depositors one rate, lends at a higher one, and keeps the difference. If a bank pays 2% on savings and charges 7% on a car loan, the 5-point gap covers its costs and profit. It also earns fees, from cards and wires to wealth management. That's why we'd steer you to a bank paying a competitive rate, so more of that spread stays with you.

qs.q: What role does the Federal Reserve play in our client's day-to-day finances?
qs.a: The Fed sets the short-term interest rate that other rates key off. When the Fed raised rates in 2022 and 2023, credit card APRs climbed above 20% and savings yields rose above 4%. Its September 2026 hike to 3.75%-4.00% does the same thing on a smaller scale. For our client, that means paying down variable-rate debt first and locking in today's higher savings yields with a CD.

qs.q: Why do banks fail if they're so regulated?
qs.a: Usually because they take on a risk that hits all at once. Silicon Valley Bank put deposits into long-term bonds, rates rose, the bonds lost value, and when depositors panicked it couldn't pay. Regulation lowers the odds but can't remove them. That's why we spread large balances so each bank holds no more than the $250,000 FDIC limit.

subs.title: Types of financial-services providers and how to choose one
what: Financial-services providers fall into a few families. Depository institutions take deposits and make loans: commercial banks (owned by shareholders, for profit), savings institutions or thrifts (historically focused on mortgages) and credit unions (not-for-profit cooperatives owned by members, often with lower fees and loan rates). Non-depository institutions don't take insured deposits: brokerage firms, investment banks, mutual fund companies, insurance companies, pension funds, finance companies and fintech apps.

There are also alternative providers such as payday lenders, check cashers, pawnshops and rent-to-own stores. They serve people with little or no bank access but charge very high effective rates. Choosing a provider means matching the client's needs (convenience, products, advice) against safety (is it insured and regulated?), cost (fees, interest rates) and trust (reputation, customer service, technology).
how: Commercial bank: checking, savings, loans, cards, business banking; FDIC-insured.
Credit union: same basic services, NCUA-insured, membership based on employer, location or group; profits return to members as better rates.
Brokerage: buys and sells securities; protected by SIPC against firm failure, not market losses.
Insurance company: pools risk through premiums; regulated by state insurance departments.
Fintech or neobank (Chime, Cash App, PayPal): usually partners with a chartered bank, which holds the money and provides the FDIC coverage.
Selection checklist: insured? fees? rates? ATM and branch access? app quality? services you'll need later (mortgage, investing)? complaints record?
nums: About 4.2% of U.S. households (5.6 million) had no bank account in 2023; the most common reason was not having enough money to meet minimum balances (FDIC National Survey of Unbanked and Underbanked Households).
Federally insured credit unions serve more than 140 million members (NCUA).
A typical two-week payday loan fee of $15 per $100 borrowed equals an APR of almost 400% (CFPB).
real: Big banks like JPMorgan Chase offer one-stop shopping (checking, mortgages, investing through J.P. Morgan Wealth Management), while online banks like Ally offer higher savings rates with no branches.
Navy Federal Credit Union, the largest U.S. credit union, serves military members and their families.
traps: A credit union is not-for-profit and member-owned; a savings and loan can be either mutual or stock-owned.
Brokerage accounts are covered by SIPC, not FDIC.
subs.say: "We'd match the provider to the need: an insured high-yield online bank for savings, a low-cost brokerage for investing, and a credit union if you want lower rates on a car loan."

qs.q: Should our client use a bank or a credit union?
qs.a: It depends on what they value, but for most young clients a credit union is worth a look. Because it's member-owned and not-for-profit, it often charges lower loan rates and fewer fees, and deposits are insured by the NCUA up to $250,000, just like FDIC coverage at a bank. A big bank wins on nationwide ATMs, apps and one-stop services. We'd suggest checking at the credit union for a cheaper car loan, plus a high-yield online savings account for the emergency fund.

qs.q: Why not just use a payday loan in an emergency?
qs.a: Because it's one of the most expensive forms of credit there is. The CFPB says a typical $15 fee per $100 for two weeks is an APR near 400%, and many borrowers roll the loan over again and again. A credit union small-dollar loan, a 0% payment plan with the provider, or the emergency fund we're building are far cheaper. Building that fund is how we keep the client from ever needing a payday lender.

subs.title: Deposit insurance and keeping money safe
what: Deposit insurance protects depositors if a bank or credit union fails. The FDIC, created by the Banking Act of 1933 after thousands of banks failed in the Great Depression, insures deposits up to $250,000 per depositor, per insured bank, per ownership category. The NCUA provides the same coverage at federally insured credit unions. Since the FDIC began in 1934, no depositor has lost a penny of insured funds.

The key phrase is 'per ownership category.' Single accounts, joint accounts, certain retirement accounts and trust accounts each get separate coverage, so a married couple can insure far more than $250,000 at one bank by titling accounts correctly. Investments are different: stocks, bonds, mutual funds, annuities and crypto are not FDIC-insured even if you buy them at a bank. At a brokerage, SIPC protects up to $500,000 (including $250,000 cash) if the firm fails, but never protects against market losses.
how: Covered: checking, savings, money market deposit accounts, CDs.
Not covered: stocks, bonds, mutual funds, ETFs, annuities, life insurance, crypto, safe deposit box contents.
Joint accounts: $250,000 per co-owner, so $500,000 for a couple's joint account.
Large balances: spread across several banks, use different ownership categories, use a sweep network like IntraFi, or hold Treasury bills (backed by the U.S. government).
Fintech apps: FDIC 'pass-through' coverage protects you if the partner bank fails, not if the app company itself fails or loses records.
nums: $250,000 per depositor, per bank, per ownership category (FDIC); the same limit at credit unions (NCUA).
SIPC: up to $500,000 per customer, including a $250,000 limit for cash (SIPC).
About 94% of Silicon Valley Bank's deposits were uninsured when it failed in March 2023 (Federal Reserve review).
real: After SVB and Signature Bank failed in March 2023, regulators used a 'systemic risk exception' to protect even uninsured deposits, but they warned that this isn't guaranteed next time.

When fintech middleman Synapse went bankrupt in 2024, thousands of customers of apps that used it couldn't access their money for months because records didn't match, a gap FDIC insurance doesn't cover (FDIC and CFPB statements).
traps: FDIC insures depositors against bank failure, not investors against market losses.
The limit is per bank, so two accounts at the same bank in the same category share one $250,000 limit.
subs.say: "Up to $250,000 per depositor at each FDIC-insured bank is backed by the U.S. government, and no one has lost a penny of insured deposits since 1934."

qs.q: Our client just received $600,000 from selling a house. How do we keep it safe?
qs.a: We'd make sure every dollar is insured or government-backed. The FDIC covers $250,000 per depositor, per bank, per ownership category, so we could split it across three banks, or use joint accounts and a sweep network like IntraFi that spreads deposits automatically. Money not needed for a year could go into Treasury bills, which are backed by the U.S. government. When Silicon Valley Bank failed, 94% of its deposits were over the limit, which is exactly the risk we're removing.

qs.q: Is the money in my Cash App or Venmo account insured?
qs.a: Only partly, and only in certain cases. Many apps hold money at a partner bank with FDIC pass-through coverage, which protects you if that bank fails, but not if the app company itself fails. When Synapse collapsed in 2024, customers of several apps were locked out for months. We'd keep the emergency fund at an FDIC-insured bank and use payment apps only for moving money.

qs.q: If I buy a mutual fund at my bank, is it FDIC-insured?
qs.a: No. FDIC coverage applies only to deposits like checking, savings and CDs. A mutual fund can lose value even if you bought it at a bank branch. That's normal for investments, so we'd only put money there that you won't need for five or more years.

subs.title: Payments, checking accounts and online banking
what: Payments move through a few rails. Card networks (Visa, Mastercard) carry debit and credit card purchases. The ACH network carries direct deposits, bill payments and transfers in batches, usually same day or next day. Wires (Fedwire) move large amounts in final, same-day transfers. Instant payment systems, The Clearing House's RTP network (2017) and the Fed's FedNow (2023), settle in seconds, 24/7. Apps like Zelle, Venmo and Cash App sit on top of these rails.

Managing an account well means paying bills on time (autopay for fixed bills), writing a check correctly when one is needed, and reconciling, or balancing, the account each month so your records match the bank's. Online accounts add security work: strong unique passwords, multifactor authentication, alerts and regular statement checks. Federal law limits your loss on unauthorized electronic transfers only if you report quickly.
how: Writing a check: date, payee, amount in numbers and in words, signature, memo. Draw a line after the written amount so no one can add to it.
Balancing: start with the bank statement balance, add deposits in transit, subtract outstanding checks; it should equal your register balance after adding interest and subtracting fees.
Bill pay: autopay for fixed bills, calendar reminders for variable ones; pay credit cards in full by the due date.
Regulation E (debit and electronic transfers): report within 2 business days and your loss is capped at $50; within 60 days, $500; after that, it can be unlimited.
Credit cards: the Fair Credit Billing Act caps liability at $50, and the major networks offer $0 liability.
nums: ACH processed 33.6 billion payments worth $86.2 trillion in 2024 (Nacha).
Zelle users sent more than $1 trillion in 2024 (Early Warning Services, Zelle's operator).
The Fed launched FedNow in July 2023; payments settle in seconds, any time of day.
real: Zelle payments are like cash: if you're tricked into sending money to a scammer, getting it back is hard, so banks tell customers to send only to people they know.
Most U.S. workers are paid by direct deposit through ACH, and the federal government is phasing out paper checks for its payments.
traps: Reconciling means matching your records to the bank statement, not just checking the balance.
Debit card fraud can drain your actual cash; credit card fraud uses the bank's money while it's disputed.
subs.say: "We'd set up autopay for the fixed bills and alerts on every transaction over $50, so nothing is missed and fraud is caught in minutes, not months."

qs.q: How often should our client check their accounts?
qs.a: At least weekly, plus real-time alerts. Federal Regulation E caps losses on an unauthorized debit transaction at $50 only if it's reported within two business days, and the cap rises to $500 after that. A two-minute weekly check in the banking app, plus a full reconciliation each month against the statement, catches errors and fraud early. That habit protects the money we're working to grow.

qs.q: Should our client use a debit card or a credit card for everyday spending?
qs.a: A credit card, if they pay it in full every month. Credit cards have stronger fraud protection, $0 liability at the major networks, and the bank's money is at risk while a dispute is resolved, not theirs. On-time payments also build the credit score they'll need for a car or apartment. If they're likely to carry a balance at today's 22% APR, debit is the safer choice until the habit is solid.

title: Income, budgeting & goals
blurb: Where money comes from, how to read a pay stub, how to set goals and build a budget, net worth, records and charitable giving.

subs.title: Sources of income and reading a pay stub
what: Income comes from work (wages, salary, commissions, tips, bonuses), from assets (interest, dividends, rent, capital gains), from owning a business (profit), and from government transfers (Social Security, unemployment benefits). Total compensation is more than the paycheck: employer health insurance, retirement matches, paid time off and stock awards can add 30% or more to the value of a job.

A pay stub shows gross pay (before deductions) and net pay (what lands in the bank). In between are mandatory deductions (federal income tax withholding based on your W-4, Social Security and Medicare, together called FICA, and state or local income tax where it applies) and voluntary ones (401(k) contributions, health premiums, HSA contributions). Year-to-date totals help you check that withholding is on track.
how: Pay frequency: weekly (52 checks), biweekly (26), semimonthly (24), monthly (12). Biweekly workers get two 'extra' paychecks a year.
Social Security tax: 6.2% on wages up to the wage base; Medicare: 1.45% on all wages, plus 0.9% on wages over $200,000 (single).
Pre-tax deductions (traditional 401(k), most health premiums, HSA) lower taxable income; Roth 401(k) contributions don't.
Form W-4 tells the employer how much federal tax to withhold; update it after marriage, a new child or a second job.
Salaried exempt employees don't get overtime; hourly non-exempt workers get 1.5 times pay over 40 hours a week (Fair Labor Standards Act).
nums: The Social Security wage base is $184,500 for 2026 and $192,300 for 2027 (Social Security Administration, announced Oct. 2026).
The federal minimum wage has been $7.25 an hour since 2009; many states and cities set higher minimums (U.S. Department of Labor).

For 2025 through 2028, workers can deduct up to $25,000 of qualified tips and up to $12,500 of overtime premium pay ($25,000 joint) from federal income tax; payroll taxes still apply (IRS, 2025 tax law).
real: A server earning $40,000 including $15,000 in tips can now deduct those tips from federal taxable income, but still pays Social Security and Medicare on them.
Many employers offer earned wage access apps (like DailyPay) that let workers get paid before payday, sometimes for a fee.
traps: Net pay is after deductions; gross pay is before.
FICA = Social Security + Medicare, not federal income tax.
subs.say: "Your $52,000 salary isn't $1,000 a week in your account. After taxes and a 6% 401(k) contribution, expect roughly $720 to $780 a week depending on your state, so we budget from net pay."

qs.q: Why is our client's paycheck smaller than they expected?
qs.a: Because deductions come out before the money arrives. Federal and state income tax withholding, 6.2% for Social Security, 1.45% for Medicare, plus health insurance and 401(k) contributions can take 20% to 30% of gross pay. A $4,000 monthly salary might deposit around $3,000. We'd walk through the pay stub line by line, check the W-4 is set correctly, and build the budget from net pay so there are no surprises.

qs.q: Should our client take the job with the higher salary or the one with better benefits?
qs.a: Compare total compensation, not just salary. A 5% 401(k) match on a $60,000 salary is $3,000 a year of free money, and employer health coverage can be worth $7,000 or more to a single worker. A $62,000 job with no match and expensive insurance can be worth less than a $58,000 job with strong benefits. We'd put both offers side by side in a simple table, which is also a great visual for this kind of decision.

subs.title: Setting financial goals and making decisions
what: A financial goal is a specific thing you want your money to do. Good goals are SMART: specific, measurable, attainable, relevant and time-bound. 'Save more' is a wish; 'save $6,000 for an emergency fund by next December by moving $500 a month' is a goal. Goals are usually grouped by time: short-term (under a year), medium-term (one to five years) and long-term (five years or more). The time frame decides where the money should go.

Responsible decisions follow a process: define the problem, gather information, list alternatives, weigh each one's costs and benefits (including opportunity cost, what you give up), choose, act and review. Behavioral finance shows that people procrastinate, overweight today versus the future and follow the crowd. Good plans work with human nature by automating saving and making the right choice the default.
how: Common order of priorities: starter emergency fund, get the full employer match, pay off high-interest debt, full emergency fund, retirement saving of 15% of income, other goals.
Short-term money goes in savings or CDs; long-term money can be invested in stocks.
Opportunity cost: $5 a day on coffee is about $1,800 a year, which could fund a Roth IRA contribution.
Needs vs wants: a need keeps you safe, housed, fed, healthy and employed; everything else is a want.
Review goals at life events: new job, marriage, a child, a move.
nums: People who automate savings save more: auto-enrollment raised 401(k) participation to around 90% of eligible new hires in plans that use it, compared with much lower rates when workers must opt in (Vanguard How America Saves).
In the Fed's 2024 survey, 63% of adults said they would cover a $400 emergency expense with cash or its equivalent (Federal Reserve SHED report).
real: Fidelity, Schwab and Vanguard let customers set automatic monthly investments, the 'pay yourself first' habit in practice.
Apps like YNAB and Monarch Money let couples set shared goals and track progress in real time.
traps: SMART goals must have a deadline (time-bound).
Opportunity cost is the value of the next-best alternative, not the total of all alternatives.
subs.say: "Let's turn 'save more' into a SMART goal: $6,000 in an emergency fund by December 2027, $500 a month, moved automatically the day after payday."

qs.q: How will our client stay motivated to stick with this plan?
qs.a: By making it automatic and making progress visible. We'd schedule transfers the day after payday so saving happens before they can spend it. That's how auto-enrollment pushed 401(k) participation to about 90% in plans that use it. Then they'd see a simple progress bar toward each goal and get a quarterly check-in with us. Small wins, like hitting the first $1,000, keep people going.

qs.q: What should our client do first: pay off debt or start investing?
qs.a: Both, in a specific order. First a starter emergency fund of about $1,000 so a surprise doesn't go on a credit card. Next, contribute enough to get the full employer match, because a 50% match is an instant 50% return. Then attack any debt above about 8%, like a 22% credit card, before investing more. That order gives the highest guaranteed return on every dollar.

subs.title: Building a personal budget that works
what: A budget is a plan for how you'll spend and save your income over a period, usually a month. It starts with net income, then lists fixed expenses (rent, insurance, loan payments), variable expenses (groceries, gas, entertainment) and savings goals. Comparing what you planned with what actually happened, a variance, shows where to adjust. A budget doesn't limit freedom; it decides ahead of time where money goes, so it isn't wasted.

There are several methods. The 50/30/20 rule puts about 50% of after-tax income toward needs, 30% toward wants and 20% toward savings and extra debt payments. Zero-based budgeting gives every dollar a job until income minus planned spending equals zero. The envelope method (now often digital) caps spending by category. 'Pay yourself first' moves savings out before anything else. The best method is the one the client will actually follow.
how: Step 1: find monthly net income (use the lowest typical month if income varies).
Step 2: list fixed costs, then average the variable ones from the last three months of statements.
Step 3: set savings goals as a 'bill' that's paid first.
Step 4: track spending weekly with an app or a spreadsheet.
Step 5: review monthly, compare budget to actual, and adjust categories that keep going over.
Irregular income (gig work, commissions): budget from a base month and put windfalls in savings first.
nums: Housing is the largest household cost; it took about a third of average consumer spending in 2024 (BLS Consumer Expenditure Survey).
The 50/30/20 rule was popularized by Elizabeth Warren and Amelia Warren Tyagi in the 2005 book All Your Worth.
real: Apps like Monarch Money, YNAB and Rocket Money link to bank accounts and categorize spending automatically.

Many people cancel forgotten subscriptions after reviewing bank statements; the FTC's 2024 'click to cancel' rule was struck down by a federal appeals court in 2025, so cancelling can still take effort.
traps: A budget is a plan; a financial statement records what already happened.
Fixed expenses stay the same each month; variable ones change.
subs.say: "Using 50/30/20 on your $3,000 monthly take-home pay: $1,500 for needs, $900 for wants, and $600 a month to savings and debt, which is $7,200 a year working for you."

qs.q: Why does a family that earns good money still need a budget?
qs.a: Because income doesn't guarantee savings; spending tends to rise with income. A budget makes sure the family's priorities, like an emergency fund and college for their kids, get funded first instead of whatever is left over. With 50/30/20, a family taking home $8,000 a month would send $1,600 to savings automatically. The budget is what turns a good income into real wealth.

qs.q: Our client's income changes every month. How can they budget?
qs.a: Budget from a base month, the lowest typical month of income, and cover needs and minimum savings from that. In good months, the extra goes first to an income-smoothing buffer in savings, then to goals. For example, a rideshare driver who earns between $3,000 and $5,000 budgets on $3,000 and banks the rest. The buffer pays them in slow months, so the budget never breaks.

subs.title: Net worth and keeping financial records
what: Net worth is what you own minus what you owe: assets minus liabilities. Assets include cash, investments, retirement accounts, a home and a car (at what it could sell for today). Liabilities include credit card balances, student loans, car loans and a mortgage. It's a personal balance sheet. Net worth can be negative for a young graduate with student loans, and that's normal. The trend matters more than the number.

Financial records are the paper trail that lets you budget, file taxes, prove ownership, file insurance claims and catch errors. Good record-keeping means knowing what to keep, for how long, and where it's stored safely, whether in a fireproof box, a secure cloud folder or both, with a trusted person who knows where to find it.
how: Net worth = total assets - total liabilities. Calculate it once or twice a year.
Liquid assets (cash, savings) can be spent quickly; illiquid assets (a home, a retirement account) cannot without cost or delay.
Keep tax returns and supporting documents at least 3 years (longer in some cases, e.g. 6 years if income was underreported by more than 25%) (IRS).
Keep home purchase and improvement records until you sell, plus 3 years, to prove cost basis.
Keep pay stubs until you match them to the year's W-2; shred anything with an account or Social Security number when you no longer need it.
nums: Median U.S. family net worth was $192,900 in 2022, but the average was about $1.06 million, because a few very wealthy families pull the average up (Federal Reserve Survey of Consumer Finances).
The IRS generally has 3 years from the filing date to audit a return, which is why 3 years is the basic rule for keeping records.
real: After hurricanes and wildfires, families with photos of their belongings and digital copies of insurance policies settle claims faster (Insurance Information Institute).
Apps like Empower show net worth automatically by linking all accounts.
traps: Median and average net worth are very different; use the median for a 'typical' family.
A car is an asset at its current resale value, not the purchase price.
subs.say: "Your net worth today is negative $18,000, which is normal with student loans. Our goal is to make it positive within three years, and you'll see it climb every quarter."

qs.q: Why does our client's net worth matter if they're paying all their bills?
qs.a: Because paying bills shows cash flow, but net worth shows progress. A family can pay every bill and still go backward if debt grows faster than savings. Tracking net worth twice a year shows whether the plan is working. If it rises from $40,000 to $55,000 in a year, we know saving and debt payoff are on track.

qs.q: What records should our client keep, and for how long?
qs.a: Tax returns and supporting documents for at least three years, because that's generally how long the IRS has to audit. Home purchase and improvement records until the home is sold, plus three years. Insurance policies and a photo inventory of belongings for as long as they're in force. We'd scan everything into a secure, encrypted cloud folder and shred the paper copies with account numbers.

subs.title: Charitable giving
what: Charitable giving is donating money, property or time to nonprofit organizations. For individuals it reflects values and can lower taxes; for businesses it builds reputation, employee pride and community ties. A donation is tax-deductible only if it goes to a qualified organization, usually a 501(c)(3) public charity, and you follow the record-keeping rules.

Smart giving plans ahead. Donating appreciated stock instead of cash avoids capital gains tax. A donor-advised fund lets someone take a deduction now and choose charities over time. People 70½ and older can give directly from an IRA (a qualified charitable distribution), which doesn't count as taxable income. Before giving, check that a charity is legitimate and uses money well.
how: Verify a charity with the IRS Tax Exempt Organization Search, and review ratings on Charity Navigator or BBB Wise Giving Alliance.
Get a written acknowledgment for any single gift of $250 or more (IRS).
Starting in 2026, taxpayers who don't itemize can deduct up to $1,000 ($2,000 for married couples) of cash gifts to charity (IRS, 2025 tax law).
Donating stock you've held more than a year: deduct its full market value and pay no capital gains tax on the growth.
Businesses: corporate giving, employee matching gifts, volunteer days and cause marketing.
nums: Americans gave about $592.5 billion to charity in 2024, and about two-thirds came from individuals (Giving USA 2025).
The $1,000/$2,000 deduction for non-itemizers begins in tax year 2026 (IRS).
real: After disasters, scammers create fake relief charities; the FTC advises giving to established organizations and never paying by gift card or wire.
Many employers, such as Google and Microsoft, match employee donations, which can double a gift.
traps: Gifts to individuals (like a GoFundMe for a friend) are generally not tax-deductible.
You need a receipt for each gift of $250 or more.
subs.say: "Giving can be part of the plan: $100 a month to a cause you care about, and starting in 2026 you can deduct up to $1,000 of cash gifts even without itemizing."

qs.q: Our client wants to give back but money is tight. What would you suggest?
qs.a: Start small and automatic, and give time too. Even $25 a month to a verified 501(c)(3) builds the habit, and starting in 2026 up to $1,000 of cash gifts is deductible without itemizing. If the employer matches donations, that $25 becomes $50. Volunteering costs nothing and builds connections. Giving fits inside the budget as a planned line, so it never competes with the emergency fund.

qs.q: How can our client make sure a charity is legitimate?
qs.a: Check it before giving. Search the IRS Tax Exempt Organization database to confirm 501(c)(3) status, then look at Charity Navigator for how much goes to programs versus overhead. Never give by gift card, wire or crypto to someone who contacts you, which the FTC says are signs of a scam. A few minutes of checking makes sure the money actually helps.

title: Saving & investing
blurb: Why to save and invest, the time value of money, every major investment type, risk and diversification, and how to read securities information.

subs.title: Why save and invest
what: Saving means setting money aside somewhere safe and easy to reach, like a savings account, for emergencies and near-term goals. Investing means buying assets, like stocks, bonds or real estate, that can grow over time but can also lose value. Both matter. Saving protects you from setbacks; investing is how money outgrows inflation and builds wealth for long-term goals like retirement.

The key reason to invest is compounding: earnings start earning their own returns. Over decades, time does more of the work than the amount you put in. Inflation is the hidden reason not to sit in cash: at 3% inflation, prices double in about 24 years, so money that earns nothing loses half its buying power. Investing also funds the economy, because the money people invest becomes capital that businesses use to grow.
how: Emergency fund first (3-6 months of expenses), then invest for goals 5+ years away.
Match the account to the timeline: under 1 year savings; 1-5 years CDs, Treasuries or a conservative mix; 5+ years diversified stock funds.
Use tax-advantaged accounts first: 401(k) match, Roth IRA, HSA.
Automate: invest a fixed amount every payday (dollar-cost averaging).
Stay invested through downturns; missing the market's best days sharply cuts long-term returns.
nums: From 1928 through 2025 U.S. stocks returned about 10% a year on average, 3-month Treasury bills about 3.3% and 10-year Treasury bonds about 4.5% (NYU Stern, Damodaran historical data).
$200 a month from age 22 to 65 at 8% grows to about $895,000; starting at 32 gives about $387,000 (future-value calculation).
Top high-yield savings accounts paid about 4.35% APY in mid-November 2026, while many big-bank savings accounts pay far less.
real: An investor who put money in the S&P 500 at its 2007 peak and held on was back to even by early 2013 and far ahead by 2020.
Fidelity lets customers buy fractional shares for as little as $1 (Schwab from $5), so even a teenager can own part of an S&P 500 fund.
traps: Saving is for safety and liquidity; investing is for growth with risk.
Past average returns are not guaranteed future returns; never present them as a promise.
subs.say: "Saving keeps you safe; investing makes you grow. We'd do both: an emergency fund first, then automatic monthly investing into a low-cost index fund for anything five years out."

qs.q: Why should a 22-year-old invest now instead of waiting until they earn more?
qs.a: Because time is worth more than money when you're young. $200 a month from 22 to 65 at an 8% average grows to about $895,000, but starting at 32 grows to about $387,000, less than half, even though only ten years were skipped. Waiting costs one full doubling of the money. Starting small now, even $50 a month, beats starting big later.

qs.q: What if the market crashes right after our client invests?
qs.a: It probably will drop at some point, and that's OK for long-term money. The S&P 500 fell about 37% in 2008 and 18% in 2022 but recovered and reached new highs both times. Because the client invests a fixed amount every month, a drop means buying more shares at lower prices. That's why we only invest money they won't need for five or more years, and the emergency fund stays in insured savings.

qs.q: Why not just keep everything in a high-yield savings account at 4%?
qs.a: It's perfect for the emergency fund, but too conservative for 30-year goals. Savings rates move with the Fed and fell to nearly zero from 2020 to 2022. Over long periods, stocks have averaged about 10% versus about 3.3% for Treasury bills. On $10,000 over 30 years, that's roughly $174,000 versus $26,000. We'd use both: savings for safety and investments for growth.

subs.title: Time value of money (concept and calculations)
what: The time value of money says a dollar today is worth more than a dollar in the future, because today's dollar can be invested to earn interest, and because inflation and uncertainty make future dollars less valuable. Future value (FV) is what money grows to; present value (PV) is what a future amount is worth today. Moving money forward in time is compounding; moving it back is discounting.

Four things drive every time-value problem: the amount, the interest rate, the number of periods and how often interest compounds. The same ideas price bonds, value businesses, compare loan offers and decide whether to take a lump sum or annual payments. On the DECA exam you'll use a four-function calculator, so know the formulas and how to multiply step by step.
how: Future value: FV = PV x (1 + r)^n. $1,000 at 5% for 10 years = $1,628.89.
Present value: PV = FV / (1 + r)^n. $10,000 needed in 10 years at 6% is worth $5,583.95 today.
Future value of regular deposits (annuity): FV = PMT x [((1 + r)^n - 1) / r]. $100 a month at 6% (0.5% a month) for 30 years = about $100,452.
More frequent compounding grows money faster; APY shows the effect for a year (a 5% APR compounded monthly is a 5.12% APY).
Rule of 72: years to double = 72 / rate. At 6%, about 12 years.
Simple interest: I = P x r x t (no compounding), used for some short-term loans.
nums: $100 a month for 30 years is $36,000 deposited; at 6% it grows to about $100,452, so compounding adds about $64,000.
Lottery winners often choose a lump sum that is roughly half the advertised annuity jackpot, a real time-value trade-off (state lottery disclosures).
real: Lotteries advertise the annuity value; the cash option is the present value of those payments.
Car dealers who offer '0% financing or $3,000 cash back' are offering a time-value choice: compare the total cost of each option.
traps: Present value gets smaller as the interest rate or the time gets bigger.
Use the rate per period: a 6% annual rate compounded monthly is 0.5% per month for 12n periods.
subs.say: "Because of the time value of money, the $5,000 you invest this year is worth more than $10,000 invested ten years from now at the same return, after you account for growth."

qs.q: Should our client take a $500,000 lump sum now or $40,000 a year for 20 years?
qs.a: Compare present values. $40,000 a year for 20 years adds up to $800,000, but at a 6% discount rate those payments are worth about $459,000 today, less than the $500,000 lump sum. If the client can invest with discipline, the lump sum wins on the math. If they'd likely overspend, the annuity's built-in discipline might be worth more. We'd show both numbers and let their habits decide.

qs.q: How would you explain compounding to a client who isn't good with numbers?
qs.a: It's like a snowball rolling downhill: it picks up more snow because it's already big. Your money earns returns, then those returns earn returns. $100 a month for 30 years is $36,000 of deposits, but at 6% it grows to about $100,000. Two-thirds of the ending balance is growth, not money you put in. The earlier the snowball starts, the bigger it gets.

subs.title: Types of investments
what: Investments fall into a few big families. Stocks (equities) are ownership in a company; you profit from price growth and dividends, with higher risk. Bonds (fixed income) are loans to a government or company that pay interest and return principal at maturity; they're usually steadier than stocks. Cash equivalents, such as savings, CDs, money market funds and Treasury bills, are the safest and lowest-returning.

Pooled funds make diversification easy. Mutual funds and exchange-traded funds (ETFs) hold hundreds or thousands of securities; index funds simply copy a market index like the S&P 500 at very low cost. Beyond these are real estate (directly or through REITs), commodities, annuities, and higher-risk assets like options, futures and cryptocurrency. Each trades off return, risk and liquidity differently.
how: Common stock: voting rights, dividends not guaranteed. Preferred stock: fixed dividend paid before common shareholders, usually no vote.

Bonds: Treasury (backed by the U.S. government), municipal (interest often free of federal tax), corporate (higher yield, more credit risk). Credit ratings run from AAA down; below BBB- is 'junk' or high-yield.
Mutual fund: priced once a day at net asset value (NAV). ETF: trades all day like a stock, usually with lower costs and better tax efficiency.
Index fund: tracks an index; low fees. Actively managed fund: a manager picks investments; higher fees.
CD: fixed rate for a fixed term, FDIC-insured, penalty for early withdrawal. Treasury bill: 4 to 52 weeks, sold at a discount, interest free of state tax.
REIT: owns income-producing real estate and must pay out at least 90% of taxable income as dividends.
Annuity: an insurance contract that can turn savings into guaranteed income; often has high fees and surrender charges.
nums: Broad index funds commonly charge expense ratios under 0.10% a year, and Fidelity offers ZERO index funds at 0% (fund disclosures).
Roughly 9 in 10 actively managed U.S. large-cap stock funds trailed the S&P 500 over 15 years (S&P Dow Jones Indices SPIVA report).
The SEC approved the first spot bitcoin ETFs in January 2024 (SEC).
real: Vanguard founder John Bogle launched the first index mutual fund for individual investors in 1976.
Spot bitcoin ETFs gathered tens of billions of dollars in their first year, but bitcoin's price fell by more than half in 2022, a reminder of crypto's risk.
traps: Bondholders are lenders; stockholders are owners.
Money market funds are investments (not FDIC-insured); money market deposit accounts at banks are insured.
subs.say: "For a first investor, one low-cost total-market index fund or a target-date fund gives you thousands of companies in a single purchase for less than 0.1% a year."

qs.q: What's the difference between a stock and a bond, in one sentence each?
qs.a: A stock makes you a part-owner of the company, so you share in its growth and its risk. A bond makes you a lender: the company or government pays you interest and returns your money at maturity. Stocks have averaged about 10% a year over the long run with big swings, and Treasury bonds about 4.5% with smaller ones. That's why a young client holds mostly stocks and shifts toward bonds as goals get closer.

qs.q: Why recommend an index fund instead of picking individual stocks?
qs.a: Because it's cheaper, more diversified and, over time, usually wins. An S&P 500 index fund owns 500 companies for a fee under 0.1%, and the SPIVA report shows about 9 in 10 active large-cap funds trailed the index over 15 years. One company can go to zero, like Enron or Lehman Brothers, but a whole index rarely does. For most clients, an index fund is the simplest way to own the market's growth.

qs.q: Should our client invest in cryptocurrency?
qs.a: Only a small amount, and only money they can afford to lose. Crypto isn't FDIC- or SIPC-insured against losses, and bitcoin fell more than 60% in 2022 before recovering. If they're curious, a spot bitcoin ETF at a regulated brokerage, capped at around 5% of investments, limits the damage if it goes wrong. The core plan stays in diversified index funds.

subs.title: Risk, return, diversification and asset allocation
what: Every investment balances risk and return: to get higher expected returns, you accept more ups and downs and a chance of loss. Risk comes in several forms: market risk (the whole market falls), interest-rate risk (bond prices fall when rates rise), inflation risk (returns don't keep up with prices), credit or default risk (the borrower doesn't pay), liquidity risk (you can't sell quickly at a fair price), business risk (one company fails) and currency risk (foreign investments lose value when the dollar strengthens).

Diversification, spreading money across many investments that don't move together, reduces risk without giving up much return. Asset allocation, the mix of stocks, bonds and cash, is the biggest driver of a portfolio's behavior. It should fit the client's time horizon and risk tolerance. Rebalancing, moving back to the target mix once or twice a year, keeps risk from drifting.
how: Risk tolerance: how much loss the client can stand emotionally. Risk capacity: how much loss they can afford financially. Plan to the lower of the two.
Time horizon: the longer the goal, the more stock risk the client can take, because there's time to recover.
A rough rule of thumb: hold about '110 minus your age' percent in stocks; target-date funds automate a similar glide path.
Diversify across companies, industries, countries and asset classes; avoid concentrating in your employer's stock.
Rebalance by selling what grew and buying what lagged; doing it in retirement accounts avoids taxes.
nums: In 2022 both stocks and bonds fell: the S&P 500 lost about 18% and the Bloomberg U.S. Aggregate Bond Index about 13%, a rare year when diversification across those two didn't help.
Enron employees held a large share of their 401(k)s in Enron stock; when it collapsed in 2001, many lost most of their retirement savings.
real: Bed Bath & Beyond, once a market favorite, went bankrupt in 2023; investors who owned it inside an index fund barely noticed, while those who owned only that stock lost everything.
Lehman Brothers went from investment bank to bankruptcy in 2008; diversified investors recovered with the market.
traps: Diversification lowers company-specific risk; it can't remove market risk.
Higher risk means a higher expected return, not a guaranteed one.
subs.say: "We won't bet your future on one company. A diversified fund spreads your money across thousands, so if one fails, like Bed Bath & Beyond in 2023, you barely feel it."

qs.q: How do you decide how much risk our client should take?
qs.a: We look at two things: their time horizon and how they'd react to a drop. A 25-year-old investing for retirement has 40 years to recover, so 80% to 90% in stocks makes sense. Money for a house in three years belongs mostly in CDs or Treasuries. We'd also ask, 'If your $10,000 fell to $7,000 in a bad year, would you sell?' If yes, we dial the stock share down, because the best plan is the one they'll stick with.

qs.q: Our client wants to put everything into their employer's stock because the company is doing well. Thoughts?
qs.a: We'd advise against putting more than about 10% in any one stock, especially your employer's. If the company struggles, you could lose your job and your savings at the same time. That happened to Enron employees in 2001. Keep the employer stock you get as a match, and put new money into a diversified index fund. It's about not doubling up on one risk.

subs.title: Sources of securities information and reading a securities table
what: Investors need reliable information to make decisions. The most important primary sources are the documents companies must file with the SEC on its free EDGAR system: the 10-K (annual report with audited financial statements), the 10-Q (quarterly report), the 8-K (major events, like a CEO leaving or a merger) and the proxy statement (executive pay and board elections). A fund's prospectus explains its goals, risks and fees. Secondary sources include financial news, brokerage research, Morningstar ratings and stock screeners.

A securities table or stock quote summarizes trading: ticker symbol, last price, change, volume, the day's high and low, the 52-week range, dividend and yield, the price-to-earnings (P/E) ratio and market capitalization. Reading it helps judge whether a stock is cheap or expensive relative to its earnings, how much income it pays and how volatile it's been.
how: Dividend yield = annual dividend / price. A $1.00 dividend on a $50 stock is a 2% yield.
P/E ratio = price / earnings per share. $50 / $2.50 EPS = 20 times earnings.
Market cap = share price x shares outstanding (large-cap generally above $10 billion).
Volume = shares traded that day; unusual volume often signals news.
Bond prices are quoted as a percent of face value: a quote of 98.5 on a $1,000 bond means $985.
Mutual funds are quoted by net asset value (NAV), set once a day after markets close.
nums: Every public company's filings are free on SEC EDGAR, the same documents professional analysts use (SEC).
FINRA's free Fund Analyzer compares mutual fund and ETF fees and shows their dollar cost over time (FINRA).
real: In 2021, GameStop's trading volume and price jumped wildly on social-media buzz, far beyond what its financial statements supported; investors who bought at the peak lost heavily.
Companies must file an 8-K within four business days of major events, so news like a CEO resignation appears on EDGAR quickly.
traps: A high P/E isn't automatically 'bad'; it can mean investors expect fast growth.
Yield falls when price rises if the dividend stays the same.
subs.say: "Before investing, we'd read the company's 10-K on SEC EDGAR, the same source Wall Street analysts use, rather than relying on social media hype."

qs.q: Where should our client get trustworthy investing information?
qs.a: Primary sources first. Companies' 10-K and 10-Q filings are free on SEC EDGAR, and Investor.gov and FINRA explain products and check advisors. Morningstar and established financial news add analysis. Social media is where the 2021 GameStop frenzy started, and late buyers lost a lot, so it's a place for ideas, never for decisions. We'd teach the client to check any claim against an official filing.

qs.q: How would you explain a P/E ratio to a client?
qs.a: It's how many dollars investors pay for each dollar of a company's yearly profit. A $50 stock earning $2.50 a share has a P/E of 20. A high P/E means investors expect fast growth, and a low one can mean a bargain or a problem. Comparing a company's P/E with others in its industry is a quick first check on whether it's priced reasonably.

title: Financial markets & the economy
blurb: The types of financial markets, how the Fed and interest rates work, inflation, economic indicators and the business cycle, and financial globalization.

subs.title: Types of financial markets
what: Financial markets bring together people who have money and people who need it. The money market trades short-term debt (a year or less), such as Treasury bills, commercial paper, bank CDs and repurchase agreements; it's where governments, banks and companies manage cash. The capital market trades long-term securities, stocks and bonds, that fund growth like new factories or government projects.

Markets are also split by stage. In the primary market, securities are sold for the first time (an IPO or a new bond issue), and the money goes to the issuer. In the secondary market (the NYSE, Nasdaq), investors trade with each other, which gives securities liquidity. Other markets include foreign exchange (currencies), commodities (oil, wheat, gold, often through futures), derivatives (options, futures, swaps), the mortgage market and the insurance market, where risk is bought and sold.
how: Money market: short-term, low risk, high liquidity. Capital market: long-term, higher risk and return.
Exchanges (NYSE, Nasdaq) list securities with rules and transparency; over-the-counter (OTC) markets trade directly between dealers.
Investment banks underwrite new issues in the primary market; brokers connect buyers and sellers in the secondary market.
Futures contracts lock in a price today for delivery later; farmers and airlines use them to hedge.
Insurance market: individuals and firms transfer risk to insurers, and insurers transfer it to reinsurers.
nums: The foreign exchange market is the world's largest, trading about $9.6 trillion a day in April 2025 (Bank for International Settlements Triennial Survey).
Foreign investors hold roughly $9 trillion of U.S. Treasury securities (U.S. Treasury TIC data, 2025).
real: Southwest Airlines famously used fuel futures to lock in cheaper jet fuel before oil prices spiked in the 2000s.
Reddit and Circle went public in 2024-2025 IPOs, raising money in the primary market before trading began on exchanges.
traps: The money market is about time (short-term), not about 'money market funds' only.
In the secondary market, the company doesn't receive money from the trade.
subs.say: "A CD is a money market tool for short-term safety; an index fund is a capital market tool for long-term growth. Your plan uses both."

qs.q: Why does it matter to our client which market an investment trades in?
qs.a: Because the market tells you the time frame, risk and liquidity. Money market investments like Treasury bills are short-term and very safe, right for money needed within a year. Capital market investments like stock funds are for growth over five years or more and can swing a lot. Matching each goal to the right market is the core of the plan: the house down payment goes in the money market and retirement goes in the capital market.

qs.q: How does the stock market actually help the economy?
qs.a: It connects savers with companies that need capital. When a company holds an IPO in the primary market, investors' money funds new products, jobs and factories. The secondary market lets investors sell easily, which makes them willing to invest in the first place. So when our client buys an index fund, they're both building wealth and supplying the capital that keeps businesses growing.

subs.title: The Federal Reserve and interest rates
what: The Federal Reserve has a dual mandate from Congress: maximum employment and stable prices, which it defines as 2% inflation over time. Its main tool is the federal funds rate, the rate banks charge each other for overnight loans. The Federal Open Market Committee meets eight times a year to set a target range. When inflation is too high, the Fed raises rates to cool borrowing and spending; when the economy is weak, it cuts rates to encourage them.

Rate changes ripple through the economy. The prime rate moves right away, so credit cards, HELOCs and variable loans change within a billing cycle or two. Savings and CD yields follow. Mortgage rates track the 10-year Treasury yield more than the Fed's rate, so they respond to inflation expectations too. Bond prices move opposite to rates: when rates rise, existing bonds with lower coupons lose value.
how: Fed raises rates -> borrowing costs up -> spending and hiring slow -> inflation eases (with a lag of a year or more).
Fed cuts rates -> cheaper loans -> more spending and investment -> growth, and possibly more inflation.
Higher rates help savers and hurt borrowers; they also strengthen the dollar and often pressure stock prices.
The Fed also uses its balance sheet: buying bonds (quantitative easing) pushes long-term rates down; letting them run off (quantitative tightening) does the opposite.
Businesses: higher rates raise the cost of financing expansion and inventory, which changes go/no-go decisions.
nums: The Fed raised its target range to 3.75%-4.00% on Sept. 16, 2026 and held it there on Oct. 28, 2026 (10-2 vote); its next meeting is Dec. 8-9, 2026 (Federal Reserve).
From March 2022 to July 2023 the Fed raised rates from near zero to 5.25%-5.50%, the fastest increase in four decades (Federal Reserve).
The average 30-year fixed mortgage rate was about 7.11% for the week of Nov. 12, 2026 (Freddie Mac).
real: Under Paul Volcker, the Fed pushed the federal funds rate to about 20% in 1980-81 to break double-digit inflation, causing a recession but ending the inflation of the 1970s.
Rising rates in 2022-23 caused the bond losses that helped sink Silicon Valley Bank.
traps: The Fed doesn't set mortgage rates directly.
When rates rise, existing bond prices fall (and vice versa).
subs.say: "Because the Fed raised rates in September, your credit card APR has likely gone up, so paying it off is now a guaranteed 22% return, better than any investment."

qs.q: How do the Fed's rate decisions affect our client personally?
qs.a: Directly, through their loans and savings. With the Fed's target at 3.75%-4.00% after the September 2026 hike, credit cards average about 22%, and top savings accounts pay around 4.35%. So we'd pay off variable-rate debt first, lock today's savings yields into a CD ladder, and wait to refinance any fixed-rate mortgage until rates fall. Watching the Fed's December 8-9 meeting tells us which way things are heading.

qs.q: Should our client wait for rates to drop before buying a house?
qs.a: Not necessarily. Nobody can time rates reliably, and home prices can rise while you wait. The better test is whether the payment fits the budget at today's rate, about 7.11% on a 30-year loan in November 2026, with the total housing cost under about 28% of gross income. If rates fall later, they can refinance. If the payment only works at a lower rate, they should wait and save a bigger down payment.

qs.q: Why do bond prices fall when interest rates rise?
qs.a: Because new bonds pay more. If you own a bond paying 3% and new bonds pay 5%, nobody will pay full price for yours, so its price drops until its yield matches. That's what hit bond funds in 2022, when the bond index fell about 13%. For a client, shorter-term bonds and CDs limit that risk, and holding a bond to maturity returns the full face value.

subs.title: Inflation and its impact
what: Inflation is a general rise in prices over time, which means each dollar buys less. It's measured mainly by the Consumer Price Index (CPI) from the Bureau of Labor Statistics, which tracks a basket of goods and services, and by the PCE price index from the Bureau of Economic Analysis, the Fed's preferred measure. Core inflation leaves out volatile food and energy prices to show the underlying trend.

Inflation can come from demand-pull (too much spending chasing too few goods), cost-push (higher costs for inputs like energy or wages) or too much money growth. It hurts savers in cash, people on fixed incomes and lenders with fixed-rate loans; it can help borrowers with fixed-rate debt. For businesses, it raises costs, squeezes margins unless prices rise, complicates planning and pushes interest rates up.
how: Real return = nominal return - inflation. A 4.35% savings account with 3.7% inflation earns about 0.65% in real terms.
Inflation hedges: stocks over long periods, real estate, Treasury Inflation-Protected Securities (TIPS) and Series I savings bonds.
Businesses respond by repricing, renegotiating supplier contracts, cutting waste, locking in long-term contracts and sometimes 'shrinkflation' (smaller packages at the same price).
Social Security benefits rise each year with a cost-of-living adjustment (COLA) tied to inflation.
Deflation (falling prices) can be worse: people delay purchases, which slows the economy.
nums: Consumer prices rose 3.7% in the 12 months through September 2026, above the Fed's 2% target (BLS).
CPI inflation peaked at 9.1% in June 2022, the highest in about 40 years (BLS).
Social Security benefits rise 3.6% in January 2027 because of inflation (Social Security Administration, Oct. 2026).
real: Gasoline spiked above $4.50 a gallon in spring 2026, pushing up transportation and shipping costs for businesses.
In 2022-23, many food companies cut package sizes rather than raise prices, a trend the BLS adjusts for in the CPI.
traps: Inflation reduces purchasing power; it doesn't mean every price rises equally.
Fixed-rate borrowers gain from unexpected inflation; lenders lose.
subs.say: "With inflation at 3.7%, money in a 0.01% savings account is quietly losing about 3.7% of its buying power every year."

qs.q: How does inflation change your recommendation for our client?
qs.a: It makes the 'safe' choice less safe. With prices up 3.7% over the year to September 2026, cash earning near zero loses real value every year. So we'd move the emergency fund to a high-yield account earning above inflation, keep long-term money in stock index funds that have historically outpaced inflation, and consider I bonds or TIPS for some protected savings. Inflation is why doing nothing has a cost.

qs.q: How should a small business respond to rising costs from inflation?
qs.a: Protect the margin without losing customers. First, find the true cost increase per product and reprice the items where customers are least price-sensitive. Second, lock in longer supplier contracts and cut waste. Third, communicate value. Coffee shops in 2022, for example, added loyalty perks when they raised prices. Then we'd track gross margin monthly to see if it's working.

subs.title: Economic indicators and the business cycle
what: The economy moves in a business cycle: expansion (growth, rising jobs and profits), peak, contraction (a recession if it's broad and lasting) and trough, then recovery. The National Bureau of Economic Research officially dates U.S. recessions; a common shortcut is two straight quarters of falling GDP, but the NBER looks at jobs, income, spending and production too. The 2020 recession lasted only two months, the shortest on record.

Gross Domestic Product (GDP) measures the value of all final goods and services produced in a country. It equals consumer spending + business investment + government spending + net exports. Consumer spending is about two-thirds of U.S. GDP, so confidence and jobs matter hugely. The unemployment rate counts people actively looking for work; it lags the cycle. Leading indicators, like the yield curve, jobless claims, building permits and consumer sentiment, try to signal turns ahead of time.
how: Leading indicators: stock prices, building permits, new orders, the yield curve, initial jobless claims, consumer expectations.
Coincident indicators: employment, industrial production, personal income.
Lagging indicators: the unemployment rate, the prime rate, inflation.
Business impact: in expansions firms hire and expand; in contractions they cut inventory, delay projects and protect cash.
Types of unemployment: frictional (between jobs), structural (skills mismatch), cyclical (from recessions), seasonal.
nums: Real GDP grew at a 3.4% annual rate in the third quarter of 2026, up from 2.2% in the second quarter (BEA advance estimate, Oct. 29, 2026).
The unemployment rate was 4.1% in October 2026, as employers added 165,000 jobs (BLS).
Consumer spending makes up about 68% of U.S. GDP (BEA).
real: During the 2008-09 Great Recession, unemployment peaked at 10% in October 2009 (BLS).
Unemployment hit 14.8% in April 2020 during COVID shutdowns, the highest since the data began in 1948 (BLS).
traps: Unemployment is a lagging indicator.
GDP counts final goods only, to avoid double-counting parts.
subs.say: "The economy is still expanding: GDP grew 3.4% last quarter and unemployment is 4.1%, which is a good time to build cash reserves before the next slowdown, not after."

qs.q: How should our client's plan change if a recession hits?
qs.a: The plan is built for it, so mostly it stays the course. The emergency fund covers three to six months if a job is lost. Long-term investments keep buying through the dip: the Great Recession pushed unemployment to 10% in 2009, but markets fully recovered within a few years. What we'd do is make sure cash reserves are full now, while unemployment is 4.1% and GDP is growing, so a recession is an inconvenience, not a crisis.

qs.q: Which economic indicator would you watch to judge this business decision?
qs.a: For a consumer business, we'd watch consumer spending and confidence, because spending is about two-thirds of U.S. GDP and it leads sales. We'd pair that with the jobs report, since 165,000 jobs added and 4.1% unemployment in October 2026 suggest customers still have income. If those weaken for two or three months in a row, we'd slow the expansion and protect cash. Indicators turn a gut feeling into a decision rule.

subs.title: Financial globalization and exchange rates
what: Financial globalization is the growing connection of the world's financial markets: money flows across borders in seconds, banks operate in dozens of countries, and investors can buy foreign stocks with a click. It gives businesses access to more capital and investors more diversification, but it also spreads crises quickly. The 2008 U.S. housing crash became a global financial crisis within weeks.

Exchange rates, the price of one currency in another, connect it all. Most major currencies float, set by supply and demand. Rates move with interest-rate differences (higher rates attract foreign money), inflation, trade balances, economic growth and political stability. A strong dollar makes imports and foreign travel cheaper for Americans but makes U.S. exports pricier and shrinks the dollar value of profits earned abroad.
how: Strong dollar: good for U.S. importers and tourists; bad for U.S. exporters and multinationals' foreign earnings.
Weak dollar: helps U.S. exporters and tourism to the U.S.; raises import prices.
Businesses hedge currency risk with forward contracts, options or by matching costs and revenue in the same currency.
International institutions: the IMF (stability and emergency lending), World Bank (development), Bank for International Settlements (central banks' bank), WTO (trade rules).
Trade alliances such as USMCA (U.S., Mexico, Canada, 2020) and the EU shape tariffs and rules.
nums: The foreign exchange market traded about $9.6 trillion a day in April 2025 (BIS Triennial Survey).
The U.S. dollar is on one side of about 89% of all foreign exchange trades (BIS, 2025).
real: The 1997 Asian financial crisis began with Thailand's currency collapse and spread to South Korea, Indonesia and beyond.
Big U.S. multinationals such as Apple and Procter & Gamble often report that a strong dollar cut their reported revenue in some years.
traps: A stronger dollar hurts U.S. exporters.
Globalization increases diversification benefits but also contagion risk.
subs.say: "About a third of your portfolio could go into international funds: when the dollar weakens, those holdings gain, which adds a second layer of diversification."

qs.q: Should our client invest internationally?
qs.a: Yes, a portion, for diversification. U.S. stocks have led recently, but leadership rotates: international stocks beat the U.S. in the 2000s. A total international index fund for 20% to 40% of stock holdings adds thousands of companies in other economies and a hedge against a weaker dollar. The trade-off is currency risk, which is why we keep it a portion, not the whole plan.

qs.q: How does a strong dollar affect a U.S. business that sells overseas?
qs.a: It makes their products more expensive for foreign buyers and shrinks the value of foreign sales when converted to dollars. If a company earns 1 million euros and the euro falls from $1.15 to $1.05, that revenue drops from $1.15 million to $1.05 million without selling one fewer item. The company can hedge with forward contracts, price in local currency or source costs in the same currency. Managing that risk protects the profit plan.

title: Credit & debt
blurb: How credit works, credit scores and reports, the true cost of borrowing, getting a loan, debtor-creditor law and getting out of debt.

subs.title: Why credit matters and how to use it wisely
what: Credit is the ability to buy now and pay later based on a promise to repay, usually with interest. It lets people buy homes, cars and education years before they could pay cash, helps businesses buy inventory and expand, and smooths spending through emergencies. Used well, it builds a credit history that lowers future borrowing costs. Misused, it becomes expensive debt that blocks every other goal.

There are three main types. Revolving credit (credit cards, HELOCs) gives a limit you can borrow against repeatedly. Installment credit (car loans, mortgages, student loans) is a fixed amount repaid in set payments. Open or service credit (utilities, phone bills) is paid in full each month. Credit can be secured by collateral, which the lender can take if you don't pay, or unsecured, which is backed only by your promise and so costs more.
how: Lenders judge borrowers by the five Cs: character (track record), capacity (income vs debts), capital (savings and assets), collateral and conditions (loan purpose, economy).
Wise use: pay cards in full, keep utilization under 30% (under 10% is better), never miss a payment, borrow only for things that last longer than the loan.
Truth in Lending Act (1968): lenders must disclose the APR and total finance charge.
Equal Credit Opportunity Act (1974): no discrimination based on race, color, religion, national origin, sex, marital status or age.
Credit CARD Act (2009): 45 days' notice before rate increases, no over-limit fees unless you opt in, limits on cards for people under 21.
nums: U.S. household debt reached $19.1 trillion in the third quarter of 2026, and credit card balances hit a record $1.29 trillion (New York Fed, Nov. 10, 2026).
Banks charged an average of 22.36% on credit card accounts that paid interest in the third quarter of 2026 (Federal Reserve G.19).
real: Buy now, pay later services like Klarna and Afterpay split purchases into four payments; they're convenient but can make it easy to overspend across several apps.
A first credit card secured by a $300 deposit, or being an authorized user on a parent's card, are common ways teens and young adults start building credit.
traps: Secured credit is backed by collateral; unsecured is not.
Credit is not income; it's a promise against future income.
subs.say: "Credit is a tool, not extra money. We'd use one card for a few planned bills, pay it in full automatically, and let the on-time history build your score."

qs.q: How can our client use credit cards responsibly?
qs.a: Treat the card like a debit card that builds credit. Put a few fixed bills on it, set autopay for the full statement balance, and keep the balance under 30% of the limit. Average card rates are about 22%, so carrying a balance erases any rewards. On-time payment is 35% of a FICO score, so this habit alone builds strong credit within a year or two.

qs.q: Is all debt bad?
qs.a: No. Debt that buys something that grows in value or raises your income, like a reasonable mortgage, a degree with good earning prospects or an equipment loan for a business, can be smart. Debt for things that lose value quickly, especially at 22% on a credit card, is the expensive kind. Our rule: borrow only for things that last longer than the loan, at a payment that fits the budget.

learn: New York Fed household debt report

subs.title: Credit scores and validating your credit history
what: A credit report is a record of how you've handled credit: accounts, balances, payment history, inquiries, and public records like bankruptcies. Three national credit bureaus, Equifax, Experian and TransUnion, each keep one. A credit score is a three-digit summary of that report that predicts how likely you are to repay. Lenders, landlords, insurers and some employers use reports and scores to make decisions.

Validating your credit history means checking all three reports for errors and fraud and disputing anything wrong. Under the Fair Credit Reporting Act, bureaus must investigate disputes, usually within 30 days, and remove information that can't be verified. Free weekly reports are available at AnnualCreditReport.com, the only official site.
how: FICO score: 300-850. 35% payment history, 30% amounts owed (utilization), 15% length of history, 10% new credit, 10% credit mix.
VantageScore, created by the three bureaus, uses the same range with a different formula.
Late payments and collections stay on a report for 7 years; Chapter 7 bankruptcy for 10 years.
Hard inquiries (applying for credit) can lower a score slightly for a year; checking your own credit is a soft inquiry with no effect.
A credit freeze, free at each bureau, stops new accounts being opened in your name.
nums: Free weekly credit reports from all three bureaus are permanently available at AnnualCreditReport.com (CFPB).
The average FICO score was about 715 in 2025 (FICO).
The bureaus stopped reporting medical debts under $500 and paid medical debts in 2023; a broader CFPB rule to remove medical debt was struck down by a federal court in 2025.
real: A good score can save thousands: on a $30,000 car loan, a borrower with excellent credit may pay several percentage points less than one with poor credit, which is thousands of dollars over five years.
In the 2017 Equifax breach, hackers stole personal data on about 147 million Americans, which is why freezes became standard advice (FTC).
traps: Checking your own score doesn't hurt it.
Income is not part of a credit score (but lenders check it separately).
subs.say: "Payment history is 35% of your FICO score, so autopay on every bill is the single best thing you can do for your credit this year."

qs.q: How can our client build credit from scratch?
qs.a: Start small and automate on-time payments. Options include a secured card with a $300 deposit, becoming an authorized user on a parent's card with a good history, or a credit-builder loan from a credit union. Use it for one small bill, autopay the full balance and keep usage under 30%. Since payment history is 35% of a FICO score, six to twelve months of this usually produces a solid score.

qs.q: What should our client do if they find an error on their credit report?
qs.a: Dispute it directly with the bureau that shows it, online or in writing, with copies of proof. Under the Fair Credit Reporting Act, the bureau generally has 30 days to investigate and must remove anything it can't verify. Then check the other two bureaus' reports too. If the error is an account they didn't open, it's identity theft, so we'd add a freeze at all three bureaus and file at IdentityTheft.gov.

subs.title: Calculating the cost of credit
what: The cost of credit is everything you pay beyond the amount borrowed: interest plus fees. The annual percentage rate (APR) states that cost as a yearly rate so loans can be compared, and the Truth in Lending Act requires lenders to show it along with the total finance charge. What drives the cost: the rate, the amount, the length of the loan, fees and how interest is calculated.

Longer loans have lower monthly payments but cost much more in total interest. Credit cards compound interest daily on unpaid balances, and minimum payments are designed to keep you paying for years. A good habit is to always look at the total amount repaid, not just the monthly payment, which is the number salespeople focus on.
how: Simple interest: I = P x r x t. $2,000 at 8% for 2 years = $320.
Amortizing loan: each payment covers interest first, then principal; early payments are mostly interest.
$30,000 car loan at 7% for 60 months: about $594 a month and about $5,640 of interest. At 84 months the payment drops but total interest rises to about $8,000.
$5,000 card balance at 22% paying $200 a month: about 34 months and about $1,750 of interest; paying only the minimum can take well over a decade.
Fees add cost: origination fees, balance-transfer fees (often 3%-5%), late fees, annual fees.
nums: Banks charged an average of 22.36% on credit card accounts that paid interest in the third quarter of 2026 (Federal Reserve G.19).
Federal undergraduate student loans first disbursed from July 1, 2026 to June 30, 2027 carry a fixed 6.52% rate; graduate loans 8.07%; Parent PLUS 9.07% (U.S. Department of Education).
real: By law, every credit card statement shows how long it will take to pay off the balance with only minimum payments, and the total cost (CARD Act).
Car buyers increasingly choose 72- and 84-month loans to lower payments, which raises total interest and the risk of owing more than the car is worth.
traps: A lower monthly payment can mean a more expensive loan.
APR includes fees; the interest rate alone doesn't.
subs.say: "At 22%, carrying that $5,000 balance costs about $1,100 a year in interest. Paying $200 a month clears it in under three years."

qs.q: Our client is choosing between a 60-month and an 84-month car loan. What do you recommend?
