qs.a: The 60-month loan, if the payment fits. On $30,000 at 7%, the 60-month payment is about $594 and total interest about $5,640. Stretching to 84 months cuts the payment by roughly $140 but raises interest to about $8,000, and they'd likely owe more than the car is worth for years. If the 60-month payment doesn't fit, a cheaper car is the better fix.

qs.q: How would you explain APR to a client?
qs.a: APR is the yearly price tag of borrowing, including interest and most fees, so you can compare loans fairly. A loan with a 6% rate and a big origination fee might have a 7% APR, while a 6.5% loan with no fees has a 6.5% APR and costs less. The Truth in Lending Act requires lenders to show it. We'd always compare APRs and total repaid, never just the monthly payment.

subs.title: Applying for loans and debtor-creditor relationships
what: Applying for a consumer loan means proving you can and will repay. Lenders check your credit report and score, verify income and employment (pay stubs, W-2s, tax returns), calculate your debt-to-income ratio and, for secured loans, value the collateral. Shopping around matters: rate quotes for the same type of loan within a short window (about 14 to 45 days, depending on the scoring model) count as one inquiry, and the Loan Estimate form for mortgages makes offers easy to compare.

Once you borrow, you're in a debtor-creditor relationship governed by contract and law. The creditor can charge late fees, report late payments, send the debt to collection and, for secured debt, repossess or foreclose. Unsecured creditors may sue and, with a court judgment, garnish wages. Debtors have protections: the Fair Debt Collection Practices Act bans harassment and false threats, and bankruptcy law offers a last-resort fresh start.
how: Mortgage basics: fixed vs adjustable rate, 15 vs 30 years, down payment (20% avoids private mortgage insurance), the 28/36 guideline (housing under 28% of gross income, all debt under 36%).
Cosigning makes you 100% responsible for someone else's debt.
Lien: a creditor's legal claim on property until a debt is paid.

Bankruptcy: Chapter 7 (liquidation, most unsecured debts wiped out), Chapter 13 (3-5 year repayment plan, keep property), Chapter 11 (business reorganization). Most student loans and recent taxes usually survive bankruptcy.
Collectors may not call before 8 a.m. or after 9 p.m., threaten arrest, or discuss your debt with others (FDCPA).
nums: The average 30-year fixed mortgage rate was about 7.11% for the week of Nov. 12, 2026 (Freddie Mac).
For 2025 through 2028, interest on loans for new U.S.-assembled personal vehicles is deductible up to $10,000 a year, subject to income limits (IRS, 2025 tax law).
real: Lenders' Loan Estimate and Closing Disclosure forms, required since 2015, let buyers compare mortgage offers line by line (CFPB).
Toys R Us filed Chapter 11 in 2017 hoping to reorganize but ended up liquidating its U.S. stores in 2018 (court filings).
traps: Chapter 7 liquidates; Chapter 13 repays over time.
A cosigner is fully liable, not just a backup reference.
subs.say: "Before you apply, we'll pull your free credit reports, fix any errors, and get three quotes within two weeks so they count as a single inquiry."

qs.q: How can our client get the best rate on their first car or home loan?
qs.a: Prepare before applying. Check all three credit reports for errors, pay card balances below 30% of their limits, and gather pay stubs and tax returns. Then get pre-approved by two or three lenders, including a credit union, within about two weeks so the inquiries count as one. Even half a percentage point on a $300,000 mortgage saves tens of thousands over 30 years. Comparing APRs is the cheapest win in the whole plan.

qs.q: A friend asked our client to cosign a loan. What would you advise?
qs.a: Only do it if they're willing and able to pay the whole loan themselves. A cosigner is 100% legally responsible: if the friend misses payments, the lender comes to the cosigner, and the late payments hit their credit report too. A safer way to help is a gift they can afford to lose, or helping the friend build credit with a secured card. Protecting the client's credit protects every goal in their plan.

subs.title: Controlling and paying off debt
what: Debt is under control when payments fit comfortably in the budget, balances are falling and there's an emergency fund so new surprises don't add more. Warning signs include paying only minimums, using one card to pay another, being turned down for credit, collection calls, or not knowing how much you owe. The first step is always a full list: every debt, balance, rate and minimum payment.

Two payoff methods work. The avalanche method pays minimums on everything and puts extra money toward the highest-rate debt first, which saves the most interest. The snowball method attacks the smallest balance first for quick wins, which keeps some people motivated. Tools include balance-transfer cards (0% for a period, usually with a 3%-5% fee), consolidation loans at a lower rate, nonprofit credit counseling and, as a last resort, bankruptcy.
how: Debt-to-income (DTI) = monthly debt payments / gross monthly income. Under 36% is a common healthy guideline; many mortgage lenders cap it around 43%-45%.
Avalanche = highest APR first (mathematically best). Snowball = smallest balance first (behaviorally motivating).
Nonprofit credit counselors (NFCC members) can set up a debt management plan with lower rates; beware for-profit 'debt settlement' firms that charge big fees and damage credit.
Call the lender before missing a payment; many offer hardship programs.
Stop the leak: freeze new card spending while paying off.
nums: About 6.87% of credit card balances became 90 or more days delinquent (annualized) in the third quarter of 2026, down from 7.05% a year earlier (New York Fed).
Credit card balances reached a record $1.29 trillion in the third quarter of 2026 (New York Fed).
real: Federal student loan borrowers saw delinquencies hit credit reports again in 2025 after the pandemic pause ended, and many scores fell sharply (New York Fed).
The CFPB has fined debt-settlement companies for charging fees before settling any debts, which is illegal under the FTC's Telemarketing Sales Rule.
traps: Debt settlement and credit counseling are different; counseling usually doesn't hurt credit like settlement does.
Avalanche saves more interest; snowball builds motivation.
subs.say: "We'd use the avalanche method: minimums on everything, and every extra dollar to the 24% card first. That saves the most interest, and we'll celebrate each payoff."

qs.q: Our client has three credit cards and a car loan. How do they get out of debt?
qs.a: First, list every balance and rate and stop adding new charges. Second, build a $1,000 starter emergency fund so surprises don't go on a card. Third, pay minimums on everything and put every extra dollar toward the highest-rate card, the avalanche method, then roll that payment to the next one. If they qualify, a 0% balance-transfer card can cut the interest while they pay. We'd track total debt monthly so they see it shrinking.

qs.q: Should our client use a debt settlement company they saw advertised?
qs.a: We'd be very cautious. Settlement companies often tell clients to stop paying, which brings late fees, collection calls and serious credit damage, and they charge large fees. Forgiven debt over $600 can also be taxable income. A nonprofit credit counselor that's a member of the NFCC can usually negotiate lower rates through a debt management plan without those risks. That protects the client's credit while they pay it off.

title: Taxes
blurb: How taxes work, filing a return, tax-advantaged accounts and how tax law shapes investing and business decisions.

subs.title: How taxes work: types, brackets, deductions and credits
what: Taxes pay for public goods and services such as roads, schools, defense and Social Security. Governments tax income (federal, most states, some cities), payroll (Social Security and Medicare), purchases (sales and excise taxes), property, estates and gifts, corporate profits and imports (tariffs). A tax is progressive if higher earners pay a larger share of income (the federal income tax), regressive if lower earners pay a larger share (sales taxes) and proportional if everyone pays the same rate.

The federal income tax uses brackets: 10%, 12%, 22%, 24%, 32%, 35% and 37%. Your marginal rate is the rate on your last dollar; your effective rate is total tax divided by income, and it's always lower. Moving into a higher bracket taxes only the dollars above the line, so a raise never lowers take-home pay. Deductions reduce taxable income; credits reduce the tax itself, dollar for dollar, which makes them more valuable.
how: Taxable income = gross income - adjustments - standard (or itemized) deduction.
A $1,000 credit saves $1,000. A $1,000 deduction saves $1,000 x your marginal rate ($220 in the 22% bracket).
Refundable credits (like the Earned Income Tax Credit) can produce a refund even if you owe no tax.
Nine states have no tax on wage income, including Texas, Florida and Washington; five have no statewide sales tax (Alaska, Delaware, Montana, New Hampshire, Oregon).
Federal corporate income tax: a flat 21% since 2018.
nums: Standard deduction for 2026: $16,100 single, $32,200 married filing jointly. For 2027: $16,600 single, $33,200 joint, $24,925 head of household (IRS Rev. Proc. 2026-35, Nov. 2026).
The seven rates stay the same for 2027; bracket thresholds rise about 3.2% for inflation, and the 37% rate starts above $661,375 for single filers (IRS).
The child tax credit is $2,200 per qualifying child under the 2025 tax law, now indexed to inflation (IRS).
For 2025 through 2028, people 65 and older can take an extra $6,000 deduction, phased out at higher incomes (IRS).
real: The IRS now calls the 2025 tax law the 'Working Families Tax Cuts'; it made the 2017 rates permanent and added deductions for tips, overtime, seniors and U.S.-made car loan interest.
A worker who earns $1 over a bracket line pays the higher rate on just that $1, a myth that stops some people from taking raises or overtime.
traps: A higher bracket applies only to income above the threshold.
Credits beat deductions of the same size.
subs.say: "Moving into the 22% bracket only taxes the dollars above the line. Your raise always means more take-home pay, never less."

qs.q: Our client is worried a raise will push them into a higher tax bracket. What do you tell them?
qs.a: That a raise always increases take-home pay. The U.S. uses marginal brackets, so only the dollars above the threshold are taxed at the higher rate. If a single filer earns $1,000 over the 12% line, only that $1,000 is taxed at 22%, an extra $100, not their whole income. Their effective rate barely moves. Take the raise, and send part of it to a 401(k), which lowers taxable income too.

qs.q: What's the difference between a tax deduction and a tax credit?
qs.a: A deduction lowers the income you're taxed on; a credit lowers the tax itself, dollar for dollar. In the 22% bracket, a $1,000 deduction saves $220, but a $1,000 credit saves the full $1,000. That's why the $2,200-per-child tax credit matters so much to young families. We'd make sure our client claims every credit they qualify for before worrying about itemizing.

subs.title: Preparing and filing an income tax return
what: Filing a tax return reports a year's income to the IRS and settles the difference between tax owed and tax already paid through withholding or estimated payments. Most people file Form 1040, due April 15 of the following year. Before filing, gather income forms: a W-2 from each employer, 1099s for freelance work (1099-NEC), interest (1099-INT), dividends (1099-DIV), investment sales (1099-B) and, new for 2025 sales, crypto (1099-DA), plus records of deductions and credits.

Filing status (single, married filing jointly, married filing separately, head of household, qualifying surviving spouse) sets the brackets and standard deduction. A teen with a part-time job usually should file even if not required, to get withheld tax refunded. Self-employed people pay quarterly estimated taxes and 15.3% self-employment tax on net earnings, covering both halves of Social Security and Medicare.
how: Forms: W-4 (set withholding), W-2 (wages from employer), 1099 (other income), 1040 (the return), Schedule C (business profit or loss).
An extension gives until October 15 to file, but not to pay; interest and penalties run on unpaid tax from April 15.
Failure-to-file penalty: 5% of unpaid tax per month, up to 25%; failure-to-pay: 0.5% per month (IRS).
Free help: IRS Free File for eligible incomes and Volunteer Income Tax Assistance (VITA) sites.
A big refund means you over-withheld, an interest-free loan to the government; adjust the W-4 to keep more each paycheck.
nums: Self-employment tax is 15.3% (12.4% Social Security up to the wage base, plus 2.9% Medicare) on net self-employment earnings (IRS).
Brokers must report digital asset sales on the new Form 1099-DA starting with 2025 transactions (IRS).
real: The IRS never makes first contact by text, email or social media, or demands payment by gift card; tax-season scams copy the IRS logo to steal refunds (IRS).
Gig workers on apps like Uber and Etsy receive 1099-K or 1099-NEC forms and must set aside money for taxes, since nothing is withheld.
traps: An extension extends the time to file, not to pay.
A refund isn't a bonus; it's your own overpaid money.
subs.say: "As a freelancer, set aside about 25% to 30% of each payment in a separate savings account for taxes, and pay estimated tax each quarter so April has no surprises."

qs.q: Our client just started freelancing. What tax steps should they take?
qs.a: Three things. First, open a separate account and move 25% to 30% of every payment into it, because no tax is withheld and they'll owe 15.3% self-employment tax plus income tax. Second, pay estimated taxes quarterly to avoid underpayment penalties. Third, track business expenses like software and mileage, which reduce taxable profit on Schedule C. That keeps April from becoming a crisis.

qs.q: Our client got a $3,000 refund and wants to celebrate. Any advice?
qs.a: Celebrate a little, then put most of it to work, and fix the withholding. A $3,000 refund means they lent the government $250 a month interest-free. Updating the W-4 puts that money into each paycheck instead, where it could go automatically to savings. This year's refund could fill the emergency fund or open a Roth IRA, which turns a one-time windfall into lasting progress.

subs.title: Tax-advantaged accounts
what: Congress uses the tax code to encourage saving for retirement, health care and education. Tax-advantaged accounts either give a tax break now (traditional: contributions are deductible or pre-tax, and withdrawals are taxed later) or later (Roth: contributions are taxed now, and qualified withdrawals are tax-free). Inside both, investments grow without yearly taxes on dividends and gains.

The main accounts are employer plans (401(k), 403(b) for nonprofits and schools, 457 for governments, TSP for federal workers), individual retirement accounts (traditional and Roth IRAs), health savings accounts (HSAs, which are triple tax-advantaged), 529 education plans and, since 2026, Trump Accounts for children. Each has contribution limits, rules on who qualifies and penalties for early or non-qualified withdrawals, usually a 10% penalty plus tax before age 59½ for retirement accounts.
how: Order of operations: 401(k) up to the full match, then a Roth IRA, then an HSA if eligible, then more 401(k).
Roth makes sense when your tax rate now is low (students, early career); traditional when your rate now is high.
Roth IRA contributions (not earnings) can be withdrawn anytime without tax or penalty.
HSA: deductible going in, tax-free growth, tax-free out for medical costs; requires a high-deductible health plan; the money is yours forever.
Starting in 2027, SECURE 2.0's Saver's Match will deposit a federal match of up to $1,000 into lower-income savers' retirement accounts.
nums: IRA limit: $7,500 for 2026 and 2027, plus a $1,100 catch-up at 50+ (IRS).
HSA limit: $4,400 self-only / $8,750 family for 2026; $4,500 / $9,000 for 2027 (IRS Rev. Proc. 2026-24).
real: Fidelity reports that a record number of its 401(k) savers have balances of $1 million or more, almost all built through steady contributions and employer matches over decades.
Federal employees' Thrift Savings Plan offers index funds with expense ratios of a few hundredths of a percent, one of the cheapest plans in the country.
traps: Traditional = tax break now; Roth = tax break later.
HSAs don't 'use it or lose it' like FSAs do.
subs.say: "Since you're in a low bracket now, a Roth IRA lets you pay tax at 12% today and never pay tax on the growth, even if it grows tenfold."

qs.q: Should our client choose a Roth or a traditional 401(k)?
qs.a: It depends on whether their tax rate is lower now or later. Early in a career, in the 10% or 12% bracket, Roth usually wins: they pay a little tax now and every dollar of growth comes out tax-free in retirement. A high earner in the 32% bracket may prefer traditional to cut taxes today. Many clients split contributions between both, which gives tax flexibility later.

qs.q: Our client can only save $300 a month. Which account should it go in?
qs.a: First, enough in the 401(k) to get the full employer match, since that's an instant 50% to 100% return. If any is left, a Roth IRA, where contributions can be withdrawn without penalty in a true emergency. For example, if a 4% contribution earns the full match and costs $200 a month, the other $100 goes to the Roth. Putting the money in the right accounts makes the same $300 work much harder.

subs.title: How tax law affects investing and business transactions
what: Tax law shapes almost every financial decision. For investors, profits on assets held more than a year are long-term capital gains, taxed at 0%, 15% or 20% depending on income; assets held a year or less are taxed as ordinary income at up to 37%. A 3.8% net investment income tax applies to high earners. Interest from municipal bonds is usually free from federal tax. Inherited assets get a 'step-up' in cost basis, which erases capital gains built up during the owner's life.

For businesses, tax rules affect structure and timing. A C corporation pays the 21% corporate tax, and shareholders pay tax again on dividends: double taxation. Pass-through businesses (sole proprietorships, partnerships, S corporations, most LLCs) report profit on owners' personal returns and may deduct up to 20% of qualified business income. Depreciation spreads an asset's cost over its life, and the 2025 law permanently restored 100% bonus depreciation, letting firms deduct qualifying equipment in year one.
how: Hold investments over a year when possible to get the lower long-term rate.
Tax-loss harvesting: sell losers to offset gains (up to $3,000 of extra loss against ordinary income each year).
Wash-sale rule: a loss is disallowed if you buy the same or a 'substantially identical' security within 30 days before or after the sale.
Asset location: hold tax-inefficient investments (bonds, REITs) in IRAs and 401(k)s; hold index funds in taxable accounts.
Businesses must file Form 8300 for cash payments over $10,000; online sellers must collect sales tax in states where they meet thresholds (South Dakota v. Wayfair, 2018).
nums: Long-term capital gains rates: 0%, 15%, 20%; short-term gains are taxed at ordinary rates up to 37% (IRS).
Federal corporate tax rate: 21% (since the 2017 Tax Cuts and Jobs Act).
The 20% qualified business income deduction for pass-through owners was made permanent by the 2025 tax law (IRS).
real: After the 2018 Wayfair decision, states could require out-of-state online sellers to collect sales tax, changing costs for e-commerce businesses.
Companies time big equipment purchases around depreciation rules; 100% bonus depreciation lets a firm deduct a $200,000 machine immediately instead of over several years.
traps: Short-term = one year or less.
S corporations avoid double taxation; C corporations face it.
subs.say: "Holding this stock just 30 more days moves the gain from your 22% rate to the 15% long-term rate, which saves $70 on every $1,000 of profit."

qs.q: How would taxes affect the way our client sells investments?
qs.a: Timing matters a lot. A gain on an investment held a year or less is taxed at ordinary rates, up to 37%, while one held longer gets the 0%, 15% or 20% long-term rate. On a $10,000 gain, that can be the difference between $2,200 and $1,500 of tax for someone in the 22% bracket. We'd also sell losing positions to offset gains, while watching the 30-day wash-sale rule.

qs.q: Should our small-business client form an S corporation or stay an LLC?
qs.a: It depends on profit. A single-member LLC is simple and passes profit through to the owner's return, but all of it faces 15.3% self-employment tax. Once profit is steady, often above $60,000 to $80,000, an S corporation election lets the owner take a reasonable salary and receive the rest as distributions without payroll tax, which can save thousands. It adds payroll and filing costs, so we'd have a CPA run the numbers for their exact situation.

title: Insurance & risk management
blurb: How insurance works, what people and businesses need, the risk management process, enterprise risk management and internal controls.

subs.title: How insurance works
what: Insurance transfers risk from a person or business to an insurance company. Many people pay a small, certain cost, the premium, into a pool, and the pool pays the few who suffer a large, uncertain loss. It works because of the law of large numbers: an insurer can't predict who will have a car accident, but it can predict closely how many of a million drivers will. Insurance is for losses you couldn't afford, not for small, predictable costs.

Every policy is a contract with key terms: premium (the price), deductible (what you pay first), coinsurance or copay (your share after the deductible), policy limit (the most it will pay), exclusions (what isn't covered) and beneficiary (who receives a life insurance payout). Insurers underwrite, or price risk, using data like age, driving record, claims history and location. Insurance is regulated by the states, not the federal government.
how: Higher deductible = lower premium; choose the highest deductible your emergency fund can cover.
Insurable interest: you can only insure something whose loss would harm you.
Principle of indemnity: insurance restores you to where you were, not better off.
Adverse selection: people who expect claims buy more insurance. Moral hazard: insured people may take more risk.
Insurers transfer their own large risks to reinsurers; they're rated for financial strength by firms like AM Best.
nums: U.S. insured losses from natural disasters are now commonly over $100 billion a year (Insurance Information Institute and reinsurer reports).

In California and Florida, several large insurers stopped writing new home policies in parts of the state after wildfire and hurricane losses, pushing more homeowners onto state-run insurers of last resort.
real: The January 2025 Los Angeles wildfires were among the costliest disasters in U.S. history, with insured losses estimated in the tens of billions of dollars.
Allstate (2022) and State Farm (2023) stopped writing new home policies in California, citing wildfire risk and rebuilding costs.
traps: The deductible is paid by you, before insurance pays.
Insurance covers pure risk (loss or no loss), not speculative risk like investing.
subs.say: "Insurance is for the losses you couldn't recover from. We'd raise your deductible to $1,000, which your emergency fund can cover, and use the premium savings to buy coverage that really matters."

qs.q: Why would our client pay for insurance they might never use?
qs.a: Because they're buying certainty. For a few hundred dollars a year, they avoid a loss that could cost tens or hundreds of thousands, like a lawsuit after a car accident or a house fire. The best outcome is that they never file a claim, just as the best outcome for a seatbelt is never needing it. We'd keep premiums reasonable by choosing a deductible the emergency fund can cover.

qs.q: How does raising a deductible save money?
qs.a: The client takes on the small, predictable losses themselves, so the insurer charges less. Moving from a $500 to a $1,000 deductible often cuts auto collision premiums noticeably. Over a few claim-free years, the savings usually exceed the extra $500 they'd pay in one claim. It works only if the emergency fund can cover the higher deductible, which is why we build that first.

subs.title: Determining personal insurance needs
what: Insurance needs change with life stage. A student may need only health and renters insurance. A new driver needs auto liability. A family with children needs life and disability insurance to replace income. A homeowner needs homeowners coverage. Wealthier clients add an umbrella policy for lawsuits. The goal is to cover the catastrophic risks: losing your health, your income, your property or your savings to a lawsuit.

Determining needs means asking three questions: what could go wrong, how much would it cost, and could the client afford it without insurance? Life insurance need is often estimated at 10 to 12 times annual income, or calculated as debts plus future expenses (college, years of living costs) minus existing savings. Disability insurance usually aims to replace 60% to 70% of income. Health insurance protects against huge medical bills; under the Affordable Care Act, young adults can stay on a parent's plan until 26.
how: Term life: cheap, covers a set period (e.g. 20 years), best for most families. Whole life: lifelong coverage plus a cash value, much more expensive.
Auto: liability (required in nearly every state), collision, comprehensive, uninsured/underinsured motorist; state minimums are usually far too low.
Renters insurance protects belongings and liability and often costs about the price of a streaming subscription.
Homeowners: dwelling, other structures, personal property, liability; flood and earthquake require separate policies.
Umbrella: about $1 million of extra liability above auto and home policies, usually for a few hundred dollars a year.
nums: About 1 in 4 of today's 20-year-olds will become disabled before reaching retirement age (Social Security Administration).
About 8% of Americans had no health insurance in 2024 (U.S. Census Bureau).
Standard homeowners policies don't cover flood damage; flood coverage comes from the National Flood Insurance Program or private insurers (FEMA).
real: Hurricane Helene in 2024 flooded inland North Carolina towns where few homeowners carried flood insurance, leaving many with uncovered losses.
A healthy 30-year-old can often buy a 20-year, $500,000 term life policy for well under $50 a month, a fraction of whole-life premiums for the same death benefit.
traps: Term life has no cash value; whole life does.
A homeowners policy does not cover flooding.
subs.say: "With a new baby, a 20-year term life policy for about 10 times your income makes sure your child is protected until they're grown, for less than your phone bill."

qs.q: What insurance does our young family client need right now?
qs.a: Four policies, in priority order. Health insurance for everyone. Term life insurance on each parent, about 10 to 12 times income, lasting until the youngest child is grown. Long-term disability coverage replacing about 60% of income, since one in four 20-year-olds will become disabled before retirement age. And renters or homeowners insurance with enough liability coverage. Together they protect the family's biggest asset: their future income.

qs.q: Whole life or term life for our client?
qs.a: Term for almost every family. It provides the most protection per dollar: a healthy 30-year-old might pay under $50 a month for $500,000 of 20-year coverage, while whole life for the same amount can cost several hundred. The classic advice is 'buy term and invest the difference' in a Roth IRA or 401(k). Whole life can make sense for special estate-planning needs, but not as a starter policy.

qs.q: How often should our client review their insurance?
qs.a: Once a year, and after every major life event: marriage, a new baby, buying a home, a raise or starting a business. Each one changes what they'd lose. A new home needs homeowners and maybe flood coverage. A new baby means more life insurance and naming a guardian. A quick annual review keeps coverage matched to their life.

subs.title: Insurance for businesses
what: Businesses face risks that can end them overnight: a customer injury lawsuit, a fire, a data breach, a key employee's death or a shutdown that stops revenue. Business insurance transfers those risks. Small businesses often start with a business owner's policy (BOP), which bundles general liability and commercial property at a lower price, then add coverage specific to their industry.

Some coverage is legally required: workers' compensation in almost every state once a business has employees, commercial auto for business vehicles, and sometimes professional licenses that require liability coverage. Lenders and landlords often require proof of insurance before they'll lend or lease. Advisors match coverage to the business's real exposures, such as product liability for a food maker or cyber coverage for anyone holding customer data.
how: General liability: customer injuries and property damage. Product liability: harm caused by what you sell.
Commercial property: building, equipment and inventory. Business interruption: lost income and expenses during a covered shutdown.
Workers' compensation: employees' medical costs and lost wages from work injuries.
Professional liability (errors and omissions): advice or service mistakes, for accountants, advisors and consultants.
Cyber liability: breach response, notification and lawsuits. Key person life insurance: cash if an essential owner or employee dies.
Directors and officers (D&O): protects leaders against lawsuits over management decisions; fidelity bonds cover employee theft.
nums: The average cost of a data breach was about $4.4 million globally in 2025 (IBM Cost of a Data Breach Report).
Workers' compensation is required for employers in every state except Texas, where it's optional for most private employers.
real: In July 2024 a faulty CrowdStrike software update crashed about 8.5 million Windows computers (Microsoft), grounding flights; Delta said the outage cost it about $500 million, a reminder of third-party and business interruption risk.
Many businesses learned during COVID that standard business interruption policies required physical damage, so most pandemic claims were denied.
traps: Business interruption usually requires a covered physical loss.
Workers' comp covers employees, not customers.
subs.say: "For your food truck, we'd start with general and product liability, commercial auto and a business owner's policy. One food-poisoning claim without coverage could close the business."

qs.q: What insurance should our small-business client buy first?
qs.a: Start with what could close the business. General liability for customer injuries, product liability if they sell food or goods, commercial property for equipment, and workers' compensation as soon as they hire, since it's required in almost every state. A business owner's policy bundles liability and property for less. If they store customer data, add cyber coverage, because breaches cost millions on average. Then review yearly as they grow.

qs.q: How can a business lower its insurance costs without losing protection?
qs.a: Reduce the risk itself, then shop smart. Safety training, cameras and good record-keeping lower claims, and insurers price that in. Bundling into a business owner's policy, raising deductibles the business can afford and comparing quotes through an independent agent each year all help. A restaurant that adds anti-slip mats and fire suppression, for example, can lower both its claims and its premiums.

subs.title: The risk management process and assessing an event
what: Risk is the chance that something will happen that affects goals. Risk management is the process of finding, measuring and dealing with risks so the business can still reach its goals. Pure risks can only cause loss (fire, injury); speculative risks can cause loss or gain (launching a product, investing). Risks are also grouped by source: economic, natural, human, technological, legal and reputational.

The process has five steps: identify risks, assess them (how likely, how severe), prioritize, choose a response, and monitor. The four responses are avoid (don't do the risky thing), reduce or control (lower the likelihood or impact), transfer (insurance, contracts, outsourcing) and retain or accept (absorb small losses, often with a reserve fund). A risk assessment of an event, like a conference, a concert or a product launch, applies the same steps to one specific situation.
how: Risk matrix: rate each risk's likelihood (1-5) and impact (1-5); multiply to rank; the top-right box is handled first.
Event risks: weather, crowd safety, security, vendor failure, technology failure, injury liability, low attendance, cancellation.
Controls for events: permits, insurance (event cancellation, liability), vendor contracts with penalties, backup power and venue, crowd management plan, emergency procedures.
Assign an owner to each risk and a trigger for acting (for example, 'if the forecast shows a 60% chance of storms 48 hours out, move indoors').
After the event, review what happened and update the plan.
nums: The 2021 Astroworld festival crowd crush killed 10 people and led to hundreds of lawsuits, showing the cost of weak crowd-safety planning.
Taylor Swift's three Vienna concerts were canceled in August 2024 after authorities uncovered a terror plot; event cancellation insurance and security planning exist for exactly this.
real: Airlines retain the risk of small delays but transfer catastrophic aircraft liability to insurers and reinsurers.
Major sports leagues buy event cancellation insurance; many policies written after 2020 now exclude pandemics.
traps: Insurance is risk transfer, not risk avoidance.
Assessment = likelihood x impact.
subs.say: "We'd rank each risk on a simple likelihood-times-impact matrix, fix the top three first, and insure what we can't control."

qs.q: What's the biggest risk to this plan, and what would you do about it?
qs.a: The biggest risk is the one with high likelihood and high impact. Here that's a cash shortfall in the first year. We'd reduce it with a three-month operating reserve, transfer part of it with a line of credit arranged before it's needed, and monitor it with a monthly cash forecast. If cash drops below two months of expenses, the trigger is to pause the expansion. Naming the risk and the trigger shows we've planned for it.

qs.q: How would you assess the risks of hosting a large client event?
qs.a: We'd list everything that could go wrong, rate each on likelihood and impact, and plan for the top risks. For an outdoor event, weather and crowd safety rank highest, so we'd book a backup indoor space, hire licensed security, and buy liability and event cancellation insurance. Vendor contracts would include penalties for no-shows. One person owns each risk, and we review the plan 48 hours out.

subs.title: Enterprise risk management and internal controls
what: Enterprise risk management (ERM) manages risk across the whole organization, tied to strategy, instead of department by department. The COSO ERM framework (updated 2017) has leaders set a risk appetite (how much risk the company is willing to take to pursue its goals), identify and rate risks across all units, and report them to the board. It treats risk as something that can create value, not just something to avoid.

Risk control means the policies and checks that keep risks in bounds. Internal controls are inside the company: approvals, segregation of duties, reconciliations, physical security, IT access limits and internal audit. External controls come from outside: regulators, laws, external auditors, credit rating agencies and contracts. COSO's internal control framework lists five components: control environment, risk assessment, control activities, information and communication, and monitoring.
how: Segregation of duties: the person who approves a payment shouldn't also record it or reconcile the account.
Three lines model: (1) business managers own risks, (2) risk and compliance teams oversee, (3) internal audit gives independent assurance (Institute of Internal Auditors).
Technology in risk management: AI and machine-learning fraud detection, real-time dashboards, cybersecurity tools, stress testing and scenario models.

Legal considerations: Sarbanes-Oxley Section 404 requires public companies to assess internal controls over financial reporting; large banks face Fed stress tests; privacy and data laws set security duties.
Ethics in risk management: report risks honestly, don't hide bad news, and don't let pay incentives reward excessive risk-taking.
nums: Organizations lose an estimated 5% of revenue to fraud each year, and a lack of internal controls was the top weakness in reported cases (ACFE Occupational Fraud 2024: A Report to the Nations).
Banks with $100 billion or more in assets take part in the Fed's annual stress tests (Federal Reserve).
real: Wells Fargo's sales-pressure culture led employees to open millions of unauthorized accounts; the bank paid $3 billion in 2020 and operated under a Fed asset cap from 2018 until it was lifted in 2025, a lesson in incentive and conduct risk.
JPMorgan's 2012 'London Whale' trades lost about $6 billion when risk limits were weakened, and the bank paid about $920 million in penalties.
traps: Internal controls are created by the company; external controls are imposed from outside.
ERM is organization-wide; traditional risk management works in silos.
subs.say: "We'd set clear controls: two people sign off on any payment over $5,000, and someone else reconciles the account every month. It's simple, and it stops most fraud."

qs.q: How would you prevent employee fraud in this business?
qs.a: With a few basic internal controls. Segregation of duties, so the person who approves payments doesn't also record them or reconcile the bank account. Dual approval for any payment over a set amount. Monthly reconciliations reviewed by the owner, and mandatory vacations so someone else covers each role. The ACFE says lack of internal controls is the top weakness in fraud cases, and these steps cost almost nothing.

qs.q: What is enterprise risk management and why should our client's company use it?
qs.a: ERM looks at all of the company's risks together and ties them to strategy, instead of each department managing its own. Leaders set a risk appetite, rank risks across the company and report the top ones to the board. That catches risks that fall between departments. Wells Fargo's sales goals created conduct risk no single team owned, and it cost the bank $3 billion. ERM helps the company take smart risks on purpose instead of by accident.

title: Retirement & estate planning
blurb: Retirement accounts, Social Security and Medicare, turning savings into income, and wills, trusts and passing on wealth.

subs.title: Retirement accounts and the employer match
what: Retirement planning means saving enough during your working years to support yourself for possibly 30 years or more after you stop working. Most Americans rely on three sources: Social Security, savings in workplace plans and IRAs, and, for fewer people now, pensions. Traditional defined-benefit pensions, which promise a set monthly income, have mostly been replaced in private companies by defined-contribution plans like the 401(k), where the worker carries the investment risk.

The employer match is the most powerful feature. A common formula is 50% of what you contribute up to 6% of pay, or 100% up to 3% to 5%. Not contributing enough to get the full match leaves part of your pay on the table. Vesting rules decide when the employer's money is fully yours. Self-employed people can use a SEP-IRA or Solo 401(k), and small businesses can offer a SIMPLE IRA.
how: A common target: save 15% of income for retirement, including the employer match.
Fidelity's rough guideline: have about 10 times your final salary saved by age 67.
SECURE 2.0 requires most new 401(k) plans started after 2022 to auto-enroll workers beginning in 2025, at 3%-10% of pay.
Starting in 2026, workers earning more than about $150,000 must make 50+ catch-up contributions as Roth (after-tax) contributions.
Leaving a job: roll the 401(k) into an IRA or the new plan; cashing out triggers taxes plus a 10% penalty before 59½.
nums: 401(k) employee limit: $24,500 for 2026 and $25,500 for 2027 (IRS Notice 2026-66).
IRA limit: $7,500 for 2026 and 2027 (IRS).
SECURE 2.0's Saver's Match begins in 2027: eligible lower- and moderate-income savers get a federal deposit of 50% of contributions, up to $1,000 a year, in their retirement account.
real: Fidelity reported record numbers of 401(k) millionaires in 2025, nearly all built by steady saving over decades rather than stock picking.
General Motors, IBM and many others closed or froze traditional pensions over the past two decades, shifting retirement saving onto workers' 401(k)s.
traps: 401(k) is employer-sponsored; an IRA is opened by the individual.
Vesting applies to employer contributions, never to your own.
subs.say: "Your employer matches 100% of the first 4% you put in. Contributing less than 4% is turning down a raise."

qs.q: How much should our client save for retirement?
qs.a: Aim for 15% of pay, counting the employer match, starting as early as possible. If they can't do that now, start with enough to get the full match and raise it 1% every year with each raise, so they never feel the cut. A 25-year-old earning $50,000 who saves 15% and earns about 7% could have well over $1 million by 67. The key is starting now and automating the increases.

qs.q: Our client is changing jobs. What should they do with their old 401(k)?
qs.a: Don't cash it out. Taking $20,000 out before 59½ could cost 10% in penalty plus income tax, possibly $6,000 or more, and it loses decades of growth. Instead, roll it directly into the new employer's plan or an IRA at a low-cost brokerage, where they can pick index funds. A direct rollover avoids withholding and keeps every dollar growing for retirement.

subs.title: Social Security and Medicare
what: Social Security is a federal program, funded by payroll taxes, that pays retirement, disability and survivor benefits. Workers earn credits (up to four a year) and need 40 credits, about 10 years of work, to qualify for retirement benefits. The benefit is based on your highest 35 years of earnings, adjusted for wage growth. It's designed to replace about 40% of an average worker's pre-retirement income, so it's a foundation, not a full plan.

When you claim matters. Full retirement age is 67 for anyone born in 1960 or later. Claiming at 62 cuts the benefit permanently by up to 30%; waiting past full retirement age adds 8% a year until 70. Benefits rise each year with a cost-of-living adjustment. Medicare, the federal health program for people 65 and older, has Part A (hospital), Part B (doctors), Part D (prescription drugs) and Medicare Advantage (Part C), private plans that bundle the others.
how: Check your earnings record and benefit estimate at ssa.gov/myaccount; errors can lower benefits.
Waiting from 62 to 70 can raise the monthly benefit by about 75% or more.
Spouses can receive up to 50% of the other spouse's full benefit; survivors can receive the deceased spouse's benefit.
If you claim early and keep working, the earnings test temporarily withholds some benefits above a limit.
Medicare enrollment starts three months before turning 65; signing up late for Part B can mean a permanent penalty.
nums: Benefits rise 3.6% starting January 2027 (Social Security Administration, Oct. 2026).
The 2027 earnings-test limits are $25,560 a year (under full retirement age) and $67,920 (in the year you reach it) (SSA).

The 2025 Trustees Report projected the retirement trust fund would be depleted in 2033, after which incoming taxes could pay about 77% of scheduled benefits unless Congress acts (Social Security Trustees).
real: More than 70 million Americans receive Social Security or SSI benefits each month (SSA).
In 1983 Congress fixed a looming shortfall by raising the retirement age gradually from 65 to 67 and taxing some benefits; a similar fix is likely needed again before 2033.
traps: Full retirement age is 67 for people born in 1960 or later, not 65.
Medicare (65+) is different from Medicaid (low-income).
subs.say: "Social Security is a base, not the whole plan: it replaces about 40% of an average income, so your 401(k) and Roth IRA fill the rest."

qs.q: Will Social Security still be there for young people like our client?
qs.a: Yes, but probably not at 100% unless Congress acts. The 2025 Trustees Report projects the retirement trust fund runs short in 2033, after which payroll taxes would still cover about 77% of promised benefits. It won't disappear, because workers keep paying in. Congress fixed a similar problem in 1983. Our plan treats Social Security as a base and builds the rest through the client's own 401(k) and Roth IRA, so they're secure either way.

qs.q: When should our client start taking Social Security?
qs.a: If they're healthy and can afford to wait, later is usually better. Claiming at 62 permanently cuts the benefit by up to 30%, while each year after full retirement age, 67 for anyone born in 1960 or later, adds 8% until 70. Waiting from 62 to 70 can raise the monthly check by about 75%. A married higher earner who waits also gives the surviving spouse a bigger benefit. We'd use their SSA estimate and health to pick the age.

subs.title: Turning savings into retirement income
what: Saving is only half of retirement planning; the other half is making the money last. Retirees face longevity risk (outliving savings), inflation risk (rising costs over 30 years), market risk and sequence-of-returns risk: a market crash early in retirement does far more damage than the same crash later, because withdrawals lock in losses. A withdrawal strategy decides how much to take each year and from which accounts.

A common starting point is the 4% rule from researcher William Bengen (1994): withdraw 4% of savings in year one, then adjust for inflation, and historically the money lasted at least 30 years. Retirees also combine guaranteed income (Social Security, pensions, annuities) to cover essential expenses with investments for everything else. Required minimum distributions (RMDs) force withdrawals from traditional accounts starting at age 73 (75 for people born in 1960 or later).
how: Income need: many planners estimate 70% to 80% of pre-retirement income.
Bucket strategy: 1-2 years of spending in cash, the next several years in bonds, the rest in stocks for growth.
Withdrawal order often used: RMDs first, then taxable accounts, then traditional, then Roth (varies by tax situation).
Annuities can guarantee lifetime income but may have high fees; compare carefully.
Roth IRAs have no RMDs for the original owner, which helps with taxes and passing money to heirs.
nums: A $1 million portfolio using the 4% rule supports about $40,000 a year of inflation-adjusted withdrawals.
RMDs begin at 73, rising to 75 for people born in 1960 or later (IRS, SECURE 2.0).
real: People who retired just before the 2008 crash and kept withdrawing heavily saw portfolios drop far more than those who could cut spending for a year or two.
Employers are increasingly adding 'retirement income' options, such as built-in annuities, to 401(k) plans after SECURE Act changes.
traps: Sequence risk is about the order of returns, not the average.
Roth IRAs don't have RMDs during the owner's lifetime; traditional IRAs do.
subs.say: "Using the 4% rule, your $800,000 would support about $32,000 a year, and with your $28,000 of Social Security that covers the $60,000 you need."

qs.q: How do we make sure our client doesn't run out of money in retirement?
qs.a: Combine guaranteed income with a careful withdrawal rate. Social Security, delayed if possible, plus any pension covers essentials like housing and food. Investments cover the rest at about a 4% starting withdrawal, adjusted for inflation, which has historically lasted 30 years. Keeping one to two years of spending in cash means they never have to sell stocks in a crash. We'd review yearly and trim withdrawals after a bad market year.

qs.q: Should our retiring client buy an annuity?
qs.a: Possibly for part of their savings, to cover essential expenses with guaranteed lifetime income. A simple immediate annuity turns a lump sum into a monthly check for life, which protects against outliving their money. But many annuities have high fees and surrender charges, so we'd compare a low-cost immediate annuity and avoid complex variable products. Covering essentials with Social Security plus a modest annuity lets the rest stay invested for growth.

subs.title: Estate planning
what: Estate planning decides what happens to your money, property and dependents if you die or become unable to make decisions. It's not just for the rich. Anyone with children, a home, retirement accounts or opinions about medical care needs a plan. The core documents are a will (who gets what, who is executor, and who becomes guardian of minor children), a durable financial power of attorney, a health care proxy and an advance directive or living will.

Many assets pass outside the will. Beneficiary designations on life insurance, 401(k)s and IRAs, and 'transfer on death' or 'payable on death' labels on accounts, go straight to the named person and override the will, so they must be kept up to date. Trusts, such as a revocable living trust, can avoid probate (the public court process of settling an estate), manage money for children and keep details private. Without a will, state law decides who inherits and a court picks a guardian.
how: Name contingent (backup) beneficiaries on every account.
Review documents after marriage, divorce, a birth or death, a move to a new state or a big change in wealth.
Step-up in basis: heirs inherit assets at their value on the date of death, wiping out capital gains on growth during the owner's life.
Digital assets: list accounts and passwords securely, and use each platform's legacy-contact tools.
Gifts during life can reduce an estate; each person can give a set amount per recipient per year with no gift tax return.
nums: Federal estate tax exemption: $15 million per person for 2026 and $15.48 million for 2027; annual gift exclusion: $19,000 per recipient for 2026 and $20,000 for 2027 (IRS Rev. Proc. 2026-35).
Only a small fraction of estates owe federal estate tax, but every family needs a will, guardians and beneficiary designations.
real: Prince died in 2016 without a will; his estate took about six years and a long court fight to settle.
Aretha Franklin left handwritten wills, one found in her couch cushions; a 2023 jury ruled on which one counted, years after her 2018 death.
traps: Beneficiary designations override a will.
Probate is public and can be slow; trusts can avoid it.
subs.say: "Your 401(k) goes to whoever is named on the beneficiary form, even if your will says otherwise. Let's update it today to include your new baby as a contingent beneficiary through a trust."

qs.q: Our clients are young parents. Why do they need estate planning now?
qs.a: Because the most important decision isn't about money: it's who would raise their child. Without a will, a court decides the guardian. They need a simple will naming a guardian, term life insurance with a trust or guardian to manage the money, updated beneficiaries on their 401(k)s, and powers of attorney for each other. Prince died without a will and his estate took six years to settle. A few hours now spares their family that.

qs.q: What's the difference between a will and a trust?
qs.a: A will says who gets what and who raises minor children, but it goes through probate, a public court process that can take months or years. A revocable living trust holds assets during your life and passes them directly to heirs at death, privately and usually without probate, and can manage money for children until a set age. Many families use both: a trust for the major assets and a 'pour-over' will to catch anything left out.

title: Paying for college
blurb: Saving for education, financial aid and the FAFSA, and student loans, with the July 2026 federal changes.

subs.title: Saving for education: 529s and other accounts
what: A 529 plan is a state-sponsored education savings account. Money grows without federal tax, and withdrawals for qualified education expenses are tax-free; many states also give a state tax deduction for contributions. 'Qualified' covers college tuition, fees, books, room and board, apprenticeships, up to $10,000 of student loan repayment, and K-12 tuition. Anyone can contribute, which makes it a great gift for grandparents.

Other options include Coverdell education savings accounts (small limits), custodial accounts under UTMA (flexible but the child owns the money at 18 or 21), savings bonds and Roth IRAs. New since 2024, unused 529 money can roll into the beneficiary's Roth IRA, up to $35,000 over a lifetime, if the account has been open at least 15 years. Trump Accounts, created by the 2025 law, add a $1,000 federal seed for children born 2025 through 2028.
how: Start early: $200 a month from birth at 6% grows to about $77,000 by age 18.
A 529 can be front-loaded with five years of gifts at once without gift tax.
On the FAFSA, a parent-owned 529 counts as a parent asset, assessed at up to about 5.64%; grandparent-owned 529s no longer count at all.
If the child gets a scholarship, you can withdraw up to the scholarship amount without the 10% penalty (earnings are still taxed).
Non-qualified withdrawals: earnings are taxed plus a 10% penalty.
nums: Starting in 2026, 529 plans can pay up to $20,000 a year of K-12 expenses, up from $10,000, and qualified expenses were expanded (2025 tax law).
Trump Accounts: children who are U.S. citizens born 2025 through 2028 can get a $1,000 federal seed deposit; contributions of up to $5,000 a year began July 4, 2026 (IRS).
Average published in-state tuition and fees at public four-year colleges were about $11,600 a year in 2024-25 (College Board).
real: Michael and Susan Dell pledged $6.25 billion in 2025 to seed $250 into Trump Accounts for millions of children, showing how private donors are adding to the program.
Many states, including New York and Virginia, give state income tax deductions for 529 contributions, which adds a return on top of growth.
traps: 529 withdrawals are tax-free only for qualified expenses.
A custodial (UTMA) account legally belongs to the child at the age of majority.
subs.say: "Starting a 529 with $200 a month now could grow to about $77,000 by the time your daughter is 18, all tax-free for college, and any leftover can roll into her Roth IRA."

qs.q: How should new parents start saving for college?
qs.a: Open a 529 plan, ideally their own state's if it offers a tax deduction, and automate $100 to $200 a month. At 6%, $200 a month from birth grows to about $77,000 by 18, tax-free for qualified costs. Claim the $1,000 Trump Account seed if the baby qualifies, and ask grandparents to give to the 529 instead of toys. Retirement still comes first, because you can borrow for college but not for retirement.

qs.q: What if the child doesn't go to college? Is the 529 money wasted?
qs.a: No, there are several good options. The 529 can pay for trade school or registered apprenticeships, switch to a sibling or cousin, or pay up to $10,000 of student loans. Since 2024, up to $35,000 over a lifetime can roll into the child's Roth IRA if the account is at least 15 years old. Only as a last resort would they withdraw it for non-education use, paying tax and a 10% penalty on the earnings only.

subs.title: Financial aid, the FAFSA and student loans
what: Financial aid helps pay for college through grants and scholarships (free money), work-study (earned money) and loans (borrowed money). It starts with the Free Application for Federal Student Aid (FAFSA), which calculates a Student Aid Index from family income and assets and determines eligibility for Pell Grants, federal loans and work-study. Many colleges and states use it for their own aid too, and some private colleges also require the CSS Profile.

Borrow federal before private. Federal loans have fixed rates, income-driven repayment options and protections that private loans lack. Subsidized loans (for students with financial need) don't charge interest while you're in school; unsubsidized loans do. A smart rule is to keep total student debt below your expected first-year salary. Choosing a lower-cost path, such as community college for two years, then transferring, in-state tuition, or generous aid packages, can cut costs dramatically.
how: File the FAFSA as early as possible every year; some aid is first come, first served.
Compare offers by net price (cost minus grants and scholarships), not sticker price; loans are not discounts.
Appeal: if family finances changed (job loss, medical bills), ask the financial aid office for a professional judgment review.
Use the College Scorecard to compare graduation rates and typical earnings by school and major.

Starting July 1, 2026, new Grad PLUS loans ended, new limits apply to graduate and Parent PLUS borrowing, and new borrowers repay under the new Repayment Assistance Plan or a standard plan (U.S. Department of Education).
nums: The 2027-28 FAFSA opened in late September 2026, its earliest launch ever (Federal Student Aid).
Federal Direct loan rates for 2026-27: 6.52% undergraduate, 8.07% graduate, 9.07% Parent PLUS, fixed for the life of the loan (U.S. Department of Education).
Outstanding federal student loans total about $1.7 trillion (Federal Student Aid).
real: Many states offer free community college programs, such as Tennessee Promise, which covers tuition after other aid for eligible students.
Student loan collections restarted in May 2025 after the pandemic pause, and many borrowers' credit scores fell when delinquencies were reported (New York Fed).
traps: Grants and scholarships don't have to be repaid; loans do.
Subsidized loans don't accrue interest while you're in school; unsubsidized loans do.
subs.say: "File the FAFSA the day it opens, compare schools by net price, and keep total borrowing below your expected first-year salary."

qs.q: How can our client pay for college without drowning in debt?
qs.a: Layer the cheapest money first. File the FAFSA early for grants and work-study, apply for local scholarships, and compare schools by net price. Two years at community college before transferring can save tens of thousands. If they must borrow, use federal loans at 6.52% for undergraduates, and keep total debt below their expected first-year salary. That keeps payments manageable on an entry-level income.

qs.q: Federal or private student loans?
qs.a: Federal first, almost always. Federal loans have fixed rates (6.52% for undergraduates in 2026-27), income-based repayment, deferment if they lose a job, and possible forgiveness for public service. Private loans may need a cosigner, can have variable rates and have fewer protections. Private loans should only fill a gap after federal aid, savings and scholarships, and only after comparing several lenders.

title: Business finance & accounting
blurb: The role of finance in a business, the four financial statements, ratio analysis, budgets and cash flow, and how businesses raise money.

subs.title: The role of finance and the need for financial information
what: Finance is the business function that gets money, manages it and puts it to the best use. The finance team, led by the chief financial officer, plans (budgets and forecasts), raises capital (loans, investors), decides which investments to make (new equipment, locations, products), manages cash and working capital, manages financial risk and reports results to owners, lenders and regulators. Every other function depends on it: marketing needs a budget, operations needs equipment and HR needs payroll.

Financial information is how everyone inside and outside the business makes decisions. Managers use it to set prices, control costs and judge performance. Owners and investors use it to decide whether to invest more. Lenders use it to approve loans. Governments use it for taxes and oversight. Suppliers check it before extending credit, and employees and unions use it in pay talks. Accurate, timely information leads to better decisions; bad information leads to failures and fraud.
how: Key finance decisions: investing (what to buy), financing (how to pay for it), and dividend or reinvestment (what to do with profit).
Capital budgeting tools: payback period, net present value (NPV) and internal rate of return (IRR). Accept projects with a positive NPV.
Working capital = current assets - current liabilities; it's the cash cushion for day-to-day operations.
Users of financial information: internal (managers, employees) and external (investors, lenders, government, suppliers, customers).
Good information is accurate, relevant, timely, understandable and comparable.

The financial-information management function collects, records, stores, analyzes and reports financial data, from bookkeeping and payroll to budgeting, audits and investor reports, so decisions rest on reliable numbers.
nums: Public companies must file audited annual financial statements (10-K) and quarterly reports (10-Q) with the SEC (SEC).
Small businesses that track finances monthly with accounting software can spot cash problems weeks earlier than those that only look at year-end taxes.
real: Toys R Us was bought in a 2005 leveraged buyout that loaded it with about $5 billion of debt; interest payments starved it of money to modernize, and it filed for bankruptcy in 2017.
Costco's finance strategy of low markups and membership fees (most of its profit comes from fees) shows how finance shapes the whole business model.
traps: Finance (managing money) and accounting (recording and reporting it) are related but different.
External users need financial information too, not just managers.
subs.say: "Finance turns your idea into a plan with numbers: what it costs, how we'll pay for it and when it pays back. Our projection shows break-even in month 14."

qs.q: Why does a small business owner need good financial information?
qs.a: Because every decision, from pricing to hiring, depends on knowing the real numbers. Monthly statements show which products make money, when cash will run short, and whether the business can afford a new employee. Lenders will ask for them before any loan. A bakery owner who discovers that wedding cakes have a 50% margin and cupcakes only 15% can shift marketing to cakes. Good information turns guesses into decisions.

qs.q: How would you decide whether the business should buy this new equipment?
qs.a: Compare what it costs with the cash it will bring in, adjusted for the time value of money. If a $40,000 machine saves $12,000 a year for five years, the payback is about 3.3 years, and at an 8% cost of capital the net present value is about $7,900, positive, so it adds value. We'd also check that financing it doesn't strain monthly cash flow. A positive NPV and an affordable payment means yes.

subs.title: The four financial statements
what: Accounting records, classifies, summarizes and interprets a business's financial transactions. U.S. companies follow Generally Accepted Accounting Principles (GAAP), set by the Financial Accounting Standards Board; most other countries use International Financial Reporting Standards (IFRS). Accrual accounting records revenue when earned and expenses when incurred, not when cash moves, which is why profit and cash can differ.

Four statements tell the story. The balance sheet is a snapshot on one date: assets = liabilities + owners' equity. The income statement covers a period: revenue - expenses = net income (profit or loss). The cash flow statement shows cash in and out from operating, investing and financing activities. The statement of changes in equity (or retained earnings) explains how owners' equity moved: beginning equity + net income + new investment - dividends and buybacks = ending equity.
how: Balance sheet: current assets (cash, receivables, inventory), long-term assets (equipment, buildings), current liabilities (payables, short-term debt), long-term liabilities, equity.
Income statement: revenue - cost of goods sold = gross profit; - operating expenses = operating income; - interest and taxes = net income.
Cash flow statement: operating (day-to-day business), investing (buying or selling long-term assets), financing (loans, stock, dividends).
Statement of changes in equity: shows net income added, dividends paid, stock issued or bought back.
The statements connect: net income flows into equity on the balance sheet, and the cash flow statement explains the change in the cash line.
nums: A company can show a profit and still run out of cash if customers pay slowly or inventory piles up, which is why lenders read the cash flow statement closely.
Apple reported more than $400 billion in revenue for fiscal 2025 in its 10-K, and its statement of changes in equity shows tens of billions returned through buybacks and dividends (Apple 10-K).
real: WorldCom recorded about $3.8 billion of ordinary expenses as assets to inflate profit; the fraud, uncovered in 2002, was one reason for the Sarbanes-Oxley Act.
Enron hid debt in off-balance-sheet entities, so its balance sheet looked far healthier than it was.
traps: The balance sheet is a point in time; the income statement covers a period.
Depreciation reduces profit but not cash.
subs.say: "Your income statement shows a $20,000 profit, but your cash flow statement shows cash fell by $8,000, because customers owe you $28,000. Collecting faster is the fix."

qs.q: Our client's business is profitable but always short on cash. Why?
qs.a: Profit and cash aren't the same. Under accrual accounting, a sale counts as revenue when it's made, even if the customer pays in 60 days. If receivables and inventory are growing, cash is tied up there. The cash flow statement shows exactly where. We'd shorten payment terms, offer a 2% discount for paying within 10 days, order inventory closer to when it's needed, and arrange a line of credit for seasonal gaps.

qs.q: Which financial statement would you look at first, and why?
qs.a: It depends on the question, but for a small business we'd start with the cash flow statement, because running out of cash is what closes businesses. Then the income statement to see whether the business model makes a profit, and the balance sheet to see what it owns and owes. Together they show whether the business is profitable, liquid and solvent. Looking at just one can be misleading.

subs.title: Financial analysis and analyzing customer financial information
what: Financial analysis turns statements into insight by comparing numbers to each other, to past periods (trend analysis), to competitors (benchmarking) and to the business's own plans. Ratios are the main tool. Liquidity ratios show whether bills can be paid soon; profitability ratios show how well the business turns sales into profit; leverage ratios show how much it relies on debt; efficiency ratios show how well it uses its assets.

Financial services firms also analyze customers' financial information: income, debts, credit history, cash flow and assets. Banks use it to approve loans and set rates, advisors to build plans, and insurers to underwrite. Common techniques include debt-to-income ratios, credit scoring models, cash flow analysis of bank statements, net worth statements and, increasingly, AI models. These must be fair and explainable under fair-lending laws.
how: Current ratio = current assets / current liabilities (about 1.5 to 2 is comfortable). Quick ratio leaves out inventory.
Gross margin = gross profit / revenue. Net profit margin = net income / revenue.
Return on equity (ROE) = net income / equity. Return on assets (ROA) = net income / total assets.
Debt-to-equity = total liabilities / equity. Times interest earned = operating income / interest expense.
Inventory turnover = cost of goods sold / average inventory.
For individuals: debt-to-income, savings rate, emergency-fund months, credit utilization and net worth trend.
nums: Example: current assets $150,000 and current liabilities $100,000 give a current ratio of 1.5. Revenue $500,000 and net income $40,000 give an 8% net margin.
U.S. banks' return on assets was about 1.1% to 1.4% in recent quarters, a common benchmark for bank profitability (FDIC Quarterly Banking Profile).
real: Lenders such as banks and SBA lenders typically want a debt service coverage ratio of about 1.25 or higher: cash flow at least 25% above loan payments.
Fintech lenders use cash flow data from bank accounts to approve 'thin-file' borrowers who have little credit history.
traps: A high current ratio isn't always good; it can mean idle cash or slow-moving inventory.
Ratios mean more compared to a benchmark or trend than alone.
subs.say: "Your net margin is 8%, but similar shops average around 12%. That four-point gap is about $20,000 a year, and it's mostly in your food costs."

qs.q: How would you know if this business is financially healthy?
qs.a: We'd check four ratios against industry benchmarks. Liquidity: a current ratio around 1.5 or more means it can pay its short-term bills. Profitability: net margin and its trend over three years. Leverage: debt-to-equity, to see if debt is manageable. Efficiency: inventory turnover. If margins are falling while debt rises, that's a warning sign, even if sales are growing. The ratios tell us where to focus first.

qs.q: What information would a bank look at before lending to our client?
qs.a: Credit history and score, income and its stability, debt-to-income ratio, and assets or collateral, the five Cs of credit. For a business, the bank also wants two or three years of financial statements and tax returns, and a debt service coverage ratio of about 1.25 or higher. We'd prepare those documents in advance and fix any credit report errors first. Good preparation leads to a faster approval and a better rate.

subs.title: Business budgets and cash flow
what: A business budget is a financial plan for a future period, usually a year broken into months. It begins with a sales forecast, then builds the operating budget (expected revenue and expenses), the cash budget (when cash actually comes in and goes out), the capital budget (big purchases like equipment) and a budgeted balance sheet. Together they form the master budget. Budgets set goals, assign resources, coordinate departments and let managers spot problems early by comparing budget to actual.

A static budget stays fixed; a flexible budget adjusts costs to the actual level of sales, which makes comparisons fairer. Cash flow management is where small businesses most often fail. Even profitable firms can run out of cash because of seasonal swings, slow-paying customers, too much inventory or loan payments. Tools include a rolling 13-week cash forecast, faster invoicing, early-payment discounts, negotiating longer supplier terms and a line of credit arranged before it's needed.
how: Cash conversion cycle = days of inventory + days of receivables - days of payables. Shorter is better.
Zero-based budgeting: justify every expense from scratch each period.
Keep a cash reserve of about three to six months of operating expenses.
Seasonal businesses: build cash in the busy season, and use a line of credit for slow months.
Budget software and accounting tools (QuickBooks, Xero) connect to bank accounts and update budget-vs-actual reports automatically.
nums: An often-cited U.S. Bank study found that about 82% of small business failures involve cash flow problems.
About half of new businesses are still operating after five years (BLS Business Employment Dynamics).
real: Retailers earn a large share of annual sales in November and December, so they borrow to build inventory in the fall and repay after the holidays.
Many businesses use invoice factoring, selling unpaid invoices at a discount, to get cash immediately, an expensive but fast fix.
traps: A cash budget tracks timing of cash; an operating budget tracks revenue and expenses.
Flexible budgets adjust to actual volume; static budgets don't.
subs.say: "We'd build a 13-week cash forecast so you can see the February dip coming, and line up a $25,000 line of credit now, while your numbers look strong."

qs.q: How would you help a seasonal business survive its slow months?
qs.a: Plan the cash in advance. We'd build a monthly cash budget for the year to see exactly when cash dips, then set aside part of every busy-season dollar in a reserve. We'd arrange a line of credit while the business looks strongest, not during the slump. Then cut variable costs and renegotiate supplier terms for slow months. A pool company that saves 20% of summer revenue can cover its winter payroll without borrowing.

qs.q: How will you measure whether your plan is working?
qs.a: With a monthly budget-versus-actual report and two or three clear targets. For example: keep the cash reserve above three months of expenses, raise gross margin from 35% to 40% within six months, and cut days of receivables from 45 to 30. If any number misses by more than 10% for two months, we review and adjust. That turns the plan into something we can check, not just hope for.

subs.title: How businesses raise money
what: Businesses fund themselves with debt (borrowed money that must be repaid with interest, but owners keep full ownership) or equity (selling ownership in exchange for money that doesn't have to be repaid, but owners give up a share of profits and control). Most start with bootstrapping, using the founder's savings and revenue, then friends and family, then outside sources as they grow.

Debt options include bank loans, lines of credit, equipment financing, SBA-guaranteed loans (the government guarantees part of the loan, so banks lend more readily) and business credit cards. Equity options include angel investors (wealthy individuals), venture capital (funds that invest in high-growth startups for large stakes), equity crowdfunding and, for mature companies, an initial public offering. Grants and revenue-based financing fill niches. The right mix depends on the business's growth plans, risk and how much control the owner wants to keep.
how: Debt: interest is tax-deductible and owners keep control, but payments are due even in bad months.
Equity: no required payments, but you share profits and decisions.
SBA 7(a) loans go up to $5 million; SBA microloans up to $50,000 (SBA).
Regulation Crowdfunding lets companies raise up to $5 million a year from ordinary investors through registered portals (SEC).
Investors want a business plan, financial projections, the market size and what makes the business different.
nums: SBA 7(a) maximum: $5 million; microloans: up to $50,000 (SBA).
Reg CF crowdfunding limit: $5 million in 12 months (SEC).
real: Spanx founder Sara Blakely started the company with $5,000 of her own savings and kept 100% ownership for years by bootstrapping.
Many 'Shark Tank' founders turn down offers because the equity requested is worth far more than the cash, a real debt-versus-equity trade-off.
traps: Equity holders are owners; lenders are creditors who get paid first if the business fails.
Interest on debt is generally tax-deductible; dividends are not.
subs.say: "Instead of giving up 30% of your company to an investor, an SBA microloan of $40,000 lets you keep full ownership, and the payment fits your projected cash flow."

qs.q: Should our client take an investor's money or a bank loan to grow?
qs.a: Ask what they'd give up. A bank or SBA loan keeps 100% ownership, and interest is tax-deductible, but payments are due every month, so steady cash flow is essential. An investor's equity needs no repayment, but 25% of the company today could be worth millions later. For a profitable business with predictable sales, we'd recommend an SBA loan. For a high-growth idea with no cash flow yet, an investor who also brings expertise can be worth the equity.

qs.q: How would you convince a lender to fund this business?
qs.a: Show them they'll be repaid. We'd bring a clear business plan, three years of projections with a break-even point, and the owner's credit history and personal investment, since lenders want owners to have money at stake. We'd show a debt service coverage ratio above 1.25, meaning cash flow covers loan payments with room to spare, and offer collateral or an SBA guarantee. Lenders fund preparation as much as ideas.

title: Managerial & cost accounting
blurb: The internal numbers managers use: types of costs, break-even and marginal analysis, variance analysis, cost budgets and cost allocation.

subs.title: Managerial accounting and types of costs
what: Managerial accounting produces information for people inside the business to plan, control and decide. Unlike financial accounting, which reports the past to outsiders under GAAP, managerial accounting looks forward, has no required format and can be as detailed as a decision needs: the cost of one product, the profit of one store, the payoff of one machine. It answers questions like 'Should we raise prices?', 'Which product line should we cut?' and 'Should we make this part or buy it?'

Understanding cost types is the foundation. Costs behave differently as volume changes, relate to products differently and matter differently in decisions. The most common mistake in business decisions is letting sunk costs, money already spent that can't be recovered, drive a choice about the future. Only future costs that differ between options, differential costs, should matter.
how: Fixed costs stay the same as volume changes (rent, salaries, insurance); variable costs change with volume (materials, shipping, sales commissions); mixed costs have both parts (a phone plan with a base fee plus usage).
Direct costs trace to a specific product (the flour in a cake); indirect costs, or overhead, are shared (the bakery's rent and utilities).
Sunk cost: already spent and unrecoverable, so ignore it. Differential (incremental) cost: the difference between two options, so focus on it.
Opportunity cost: the benefit given up by choosing one option over the next best.
Product costs (materials, labor, manufacturing overhead) become inventory; period costs (marketing, administration) are expensed right away.
Controllable costs can be influenced by a manager; uncontrollable ones can't, which matters when judging performance.
nums: Example: a bakery's rent ($3,000 a month) is fixed and indirect; flour and eggs ($1.20 per cake) are variable and direct.
