Managerial reports can be daily or weekly; public companies' financial reports to outsiders are quarterly and annual (SEC).
real: Companies often keep funding failing projects because of sunk costs, the 'Concorde fallacy', named for the supersonic jet that Britain and France kept funding despite clear losses.
Amazon Web Services began as internal infrastructure; managerial analysis of its costs showed it could be sold to others at a profit.
traps: Sunk costs are irrelevant to future decisions.
Fixed cost per unit falls as volume rises, even though total fixed cost stays the same.
subs.say: "The $15,000 already spent on the old software is a sunk cost. The real question is whether the new system's lower future costs beat the old one's."

qs.q: Our client already spent $20,000 on a project that's struggling. Should they keep going?
qs.a: Ignore the $20,000. It's a sunk cost, and it's gone whatever they decide. The only question is whether the future benefits of continuing beat the future costs. If finishing needs $10,000 more and is likely to bring in $8,000, they should stop, even though it feels like wasting the first $20,000. Businesses that fall for the sunk-cost trap, like the Concorde program, lose more money. We'd decide on future numbers only.

qs.q: How is managerial accounting different from financial accounting?
qs.a: Financial accounting reports the past to outsiders, like investors, lenders and the IRS, using GAAP rules and set formats. Managerial accounting helps insiders make future decisions, with no required format and as much detail as is useful, such as profit by product or store. For our client, the 10-K shows how the company did; a managerial report shows which product to push next quarter. Both matter, but managerial accounting drives daily decisions.

subs.title: Break-even and marginal analysis
what: Break-even analysis finds the sales level where total revenue equals total costs, so profit is zero. Every unit sold contributes its contribution margin, price minus variable cost per unit, toward covering fixed costs; once fixed costs are covered, each extra unit's contribution is profit. Break-even units = fixed costs / contribution margin per unit. It's the first number any lender or investor asks for.

Marginal analysis looks at the effect of one more unit, or one more decision, on revenue and cost. A business maximizes profit by producing until marginal revenue equals marginal cost. It's used for pricing, special orders (accept an order below normal price if it covers variable costs and doesn't use capacity needed elsewhere), make-or-buy decisions, adding a shift and deciding whether to drop a product. Because of diminishing returns, the cost of each extra unit eventually rises.
how: Contribution margin per unit = price - variable cost. Contribution margin ratio = CM / price.
Break-even units = fixed costs / CM per unit. Break-even sales dollars = fixed costs / CM ratio.
Target profit units = (fixed costs + target profit) / CM per unit.
Margin of safety = actual (or expected) sales - break-even sales.
Marginal rule: keep expanding while marginal revenue > marginal cost; stop when they're equal.
nums: Food truck example: fixed costs $6,000 a month, average meal price $12, variable cost $5. CM = $7, so break-even is about 857 meals a month, roughly 29 a day over 30 days.
To earn $3,000 a month in profit: ($6,000 + $3,000) / $7 = about 1,286 meals.
real: Airlines use marginal pricing: once a flight is scheduled, an empty seat's extra cost is small, so last-minute fares can be low as long as they cover that extra cost.
Hotels and ride-share apps use dynamic pricing based on marginal demand, raising prices when demand outruns capacity.
traps: Use the contribution margin, not the full price, in the break-even formula.
Fixed costs don't change with a special order unless capacity changes.
subs.say: "At $12 a meal with $5 of food cost, each meal contributes $7 to your $6,000 of monthly fixed costs. You break even at about 29 meals a day, and everything after that is profit."

qs.q: How many units does our client need to sell to break even?
qs.a: Divide fixed costs by the contribution margin per unit. If monthly fixed costs are $6,000 and each $12 meal costs $5 to make, each sale contributes $7, so break-even is about 857 meals a month, around 29 a day. Then we'd check that's realistic: a busy lunch spot can serve 60. That margin of safety tells us the plan can work even in slow weeks. I'd sketch the break-even chart for you.

qs.q: A big customer wants a large order at a 20% discount. Should we accept?
qs.a: Use marginal analysis. If the discounted price still covers the variable cost of each unit and we have idle capacity, the order adds profit, because fixed costs are already covered. A $10 product with a $6 variable cost sold at $8 still contributes $2 a unit. We'd decline if it needs overtime or crowds out full-price customers, or if other customers would demand the same discount.

subs.title: Variance analysis and cost accounting budgets
what: A variance is the difference between budgeted (planned or standard) results and actual results. Favorable variances help profit (costs below plan, revenue above plan); unfavorable variances hurt it. Variance analysis asks why the difference happened and who can fix it, so managers can practice 'management by exception': spend time on the big surprises, not on everything that went to plan.

Cost accounting budgets are the plans variances are measured against. They are built from standard costs, the expected price and quantity of materials and labor for each unit, and include the production budget, direct materials budget, direct labor budget and manufacturing overhead budget. A flexible budget adjusts these to the actual production level, so managers aren't blamed or praised just because volume changed.
how: Variance = actual - budget (or standard). Label each one favorable (F) or unfavorable (U).
Materials: price variance = (actual price - standard price) x actual quantity; quantity variance = (actual quantity - standard quantity) x standard price.
Labor: rate variance (paid more per hour) and efficiency variance (used more hours).
Sales variances: price and volume.
Investigate variances above a threshold, for example 5% or $1,000, and assign each to the manager who controls it.
A favorable variance can still signal a problem, like cheaper materials that cause more defects.
nums: Example: budgeted materials $10,000; actual $11,200, so the variance is $1,200 unfavorable. If the standard was 2,000 lbs at $5 and the business used 2,000 lbs at $5.60, it's all a price variance: renegotiate with the supplier.
Companies in the S&P 500 explain differences between guidance (budget) and results on every quarterly earnings call.
real: When egg prices jumped during bird-flu outbreaks in 2022-2025, restaurants and bakeries saw big unfavorable materials price variances and responded with menu changes and surcharges.
Toyota's standard-cost and continuous-improvement system uses daily variance tracking on the factory floor.
traps: 'Variance' means planned versus actual, the answer to many exam questions.
Price and quantity variances can offset each other; always check both.
subs.say: "Your food costs came in $1,200 over budget, all from egg prices. That's a price variance, so the fix is the supplier contract or the menu, not the kitchen staff."

qs.q: How would you track whether the business is sticking to its budget?
qs.a: With a monthly variance report: budget, actual and the difference for each line, labeled favorable or unfavorable. We'd investigate anything over 5% and find the cause, such as price versus quantity for materials or rate versus hours for labor, then assign it to the manager who controls it. If materials ran $1,200 over because suppliers raised prices, the fix is renegotiating, not cutting staff. The report turns the budget into a monthly steering tool.

qs.q: Is a favorable variance always good news?
qs.a: Not always. Spending less than budget on materials looks favorable, but if it came from cheaper, lower-quality inputs, defects and returns may rise later. A favorable marketing variance might mean campaigns were skipped and future sales will suffer. So we'd ask why every big variance happened, good or bad. The goal is better decisions, not just a prettier report.

subs.title: Cost allocation, ABC and other uses of financial information
what: Cost allocation assigns shared, indirect costs, such as rent, utilities, IT and supervisors, to products, departments or customers using a cost driver, something that causes the cost, like machine hours, labor hours or square feet. Allocation matters because it changes how profitable each product looks, which affects pricing and which products to keep. Traditional costing uses one plant-wide rate; activity-based costing (ABC) uses many activities and drivers, such as setups, orders processed or inspections, for a more accurate picture.

Financial information also supports non-traditional uses. Lean management uses cost data to remove waste (the Toyota Production System). Six Sigma uses data to cut defects to 3.4 per million opportunities, a method Motorola developed in 1986. Sustainability reporting measures environmental and social results such as carbon emissions, energy use and workforce data, alongside financial results. These approaches connect financial numbers to operations, quality and long-term value.
how: Steps: identify the cost pool, choose a driver, compute a rate (pool / total driver units), apply it to each product.
ABC often shows that low-volume, complex products cost more than traditional costing suggests, and high-volume simple ones cost less.
Lean's eight wastes: defects, overproduction, waiting, unused talent, transportation, inventory, motion, extra processing.
Sustainability frameworks: GRI and the ISSB standards; in 2025 the EU moved to delay and narrow its CSRD reporting rules, and the SEC stopped defending its climate disclosure rule in March 2025.
Six Sigma's DMAIC cycle: define, measure, analyze, improve, control.
nums: Allocation example: $60,000 of overhead and 3,000 machine hours gives a rate of $20 per machine hour; a product that uses 2 hours carries $40 of overhead.
Six Sigma's target is 3.4 defects per million opportunities (Motorola).
real: General Electric under Jack Welch made Six Sigma company-wide in the 1990s and credited it with billions of dollars in savings.
Many large companies, including Microsoft and Apple, publish annual sustainability or environmental reports with emissions data alongside their financial reports.
traps: ABC uses multiple cost drivers; traditional costing uses one.
Allocation doesn't change total costs, only how they're divided.
subs.say: "When we allocate setup costs by activity, your custom orders turn out to cost $9 more each than you thought. That's why they've been quietly losing money."

qs.q: Why might one of our client's products look profitable but actually lose money?
qs.a: Because of how overhead is allocated. If overhead is spread by sales volume, a small-batch custom product that needs lots of setups, design time and customer service gets too little of the cost. Activity-based costing assigns costs by what actually drives them, and often shows that complex, low-volume items are the money-losers. We'd run ABC on the top products, then raise prices or simplify the ones that don't cover their true cost.

qs.q: How can financial information help a company beyond accounting?
qs.a: It can drive operations and strategy. Lean uses cost data to cut waste, like excess inventory that ties up cash. Six Sigma uses data to reduce defects, and GE credited it with billions in savings. Sustainability reporting tracks energy and emissions, which often cuts costs and meets what investors and big customers now ask for. For our client, measuring energy cost per unit could be the first step to both savings and a greener story.

title: Law, compliance & ethics
blurb: The laws and regulators of finance, compliance programs and technology, consumer protection and contracts, ethics in finance and accounting.

subs.title: Major finance laws and regulators
what: Finance is heavily regulated because it handles other people's money and because failures spread through the whole economy. Most U.S. financial law was written after a crisis. The Great Depression brought the Securities Act of 1933 (honest disclosure for new securities), the Securities Exchange Act of 1934 (created the SEC and regulates trading), the Glass-Steagall Act (separated commercial and investment banking, mostly repealed in 1999) and the FDIC. The 1940 Acts regulate mutual funds and investment advisers.

Enron and WorldCom led to the Sarbanes-Oxley Act (2002). The 2008 crisis led to the Dodd-Frank Act (2010), which created the CFPB and the Financial Stability Oversight Council, added stress tests and the Volcker Rule limiting banks' own speculative trading. The GENIUS Act (2025) created the first federal framework for payment stablecoins. Regulators include the SEC and FINRA (securities), the Fed, OCC, FDIC and NCUA (banks and credit unions), the CFPB (consumer products), the CFTC (futures and derivatives), FinCEN (money laundering) and state insurance and banking departments.
how: Illegal securities practices: insider trading (trading on material non-public information), front-running (trading ahead of a client's order), churning (excessive trading for commissions), market manipulation (pump-and-dump), Ponzi schemes.
Bank Secrecy Act (1970): banks file Currency Transaction Reports for cash over $10,000 and Suspicious Activity Reports.
Gramm-Leach-Bliley Act (1999): allowed banks, insurers and brokerages to combine, and requires privacy notices and data security.
The CFPB's funding and size have been the subject of court fights since 2025; check its current status before citing it in a roleplay.
Penalties: fines, disgorgement of profits, bans from the industry, prison.
nums: Bernie Madoff's Ponzi scheme caused about $65 billion in paper losses; he was sentenced to 150 years in 2009 (U.S. Department of Justice).
TD Bank pleaded guilty in 2024 to Bank Secrecy Act violations and agreed to pay about $3 billion, the largest such penalty against a U.S. bank (DOJ).
real: Archegos Capital's 2021 collapse cost banks more than $10 billion; founder Bill Hwang was convicted of fraud and sentenced to 18 years in 2024.
FTX founder Sam Bankman-Fried was sentenced to 25 years in 2024 for defrauding customers and investors (DOJ).
traps: The SEC regulates securities; FINRA is a self-regulatory organization overseeing brokers, under the SEC.
Front-running uses a client's pending order; insider trading uses non-public company news.
subs.say: "We're required to put your interests first, and you can check our record yourself on FINRA BrokerCheck in two minutes."

qs.q: How do regulations protect our client?
qs.a: They make firms tell the truth and put clients first. Securities laws require honest disclosure, FDIC insurance protects deposits up to $250,000, Regulation Best Interest requires brokers to act in the client's best interest, and privacy laws protect their data. The client can check any advisor on FINRA BrokerCheck. When those rules are broken, the penalties are severe: TD Bank paid about $3 billion in 2024 for money-laundering failures. Regulation is the reason clients can trust the system.

qs.q: Isn't all this regulation just extra cost for the business?
qs.a: It costs money, but it's far cheaper than the alternative. Compliance builds the trust that brings in customers, and violations cost much more: Wells Fargo paid $3 billion for its fake-accounts scandal and lost years of growth under a Fed asset cap. A firm with strong compliance can advertise it as a selling point. We'd treat compliance as part of the brand promise, not an afterthought.

subs.title: Compliance programs and compliance technology
what: Compliance means making sure a firm and its employees follow laws, regulations and internal policies. In finance, a compliance department, led by a chief compliance officer, writes policies, trains employees, monitors activity, tests controls, investigates problems and reports to senior management and the board. Key areas include know-your-customer (KYC) identity checks, anti-money laundering (AML), suitability and best-interest rules, advertising rules, privacy, record-keeping and conflicts of interest.

Compliance technology, or RegTech, automates much of this work. Software screens customers against sanctions lists, flags unusual transactions, archives every email and text, monitors trading for insider trading or manipulation, verifies identities with document scans and biometrics, and tracks new regulations. AI makes monitoring faster but adds its own duties: firms must be able to explain and test the models they use.
how: Elements of an effective program: written policies, a compliance officer, training, monitoring and auditing, reporting channels (a hotline), consistent discipline, and fixing problems that are found.
KYC: verify identity, understand the customer's business and expected activity, and update over time.
AML red flags: cash deposits just under $10,000 (structuring), rapid movement through many accounts, activity that doesn't fit the customer's profile.
Record-keeping: brokers must keep business communications, including texts, which is why off-channel messaging became a major enforcement area.
Compliance culture: leaders model it, employees can raise concerns without retaliation, and pay doesn't reward breaking rules.
nums: The SEC and CFTC fined dozens of firms more than $2 billion combined from 2021 to 2024 for employees using unapproved texting apps like WhatsApp for business (SEC and CFTC).
TD Bank's 2024 guilty plea found that most of its transactions went unmonitored for years, which let money launderers move hundreds of millions of dollars (DOJ).
real: Banks use AI transaction monitoring to flag fraud in real time; card networks such as Visa report preventing billions of dollars in fraud each year with AI.
Robinhood and other brokers have been fined by FINRA for weak supervision and customer-communication failures.
traps: Compliance is ongoing monitoring, not a one-time checklist.
Structuring (splitting cash deposits to avoid the $10,000 report) is itself a crime.
subs.say: "Compliance isn't red tape; it's what lets clients trust us. Every account goes through identity checks, and our systems flag unusual activity within minutes."

qs.q: How would you build a compliance culture at this firm?
qs.a: Start at the top and make it easy to do the right thing. Leaders talk about compliance and follow it themselves, and every employee gets short, practical training each year. There's an anonymous hotline with no retaliation, and pay never rewards breaking rules, which is what went wrong at Wells Fargo. Then technology monitors communications and transactions automatically. Culture plus monitoring catches problems early, when they're cheap to fix.

qs.q: How can technology help a financial firm stay compliant?
qs.a: It automates the work humans can't do at scale. Software screens every customer against sanctions lists, flags suspicious transactions like repeated cash deposits just under $10,000, archives all emails and texts and monitors trading for insider activity. That matters because regulators fined firms over $2 billion for unrecorded texting. We'd pair it with human review, because a flagged alert still needs judgment.

subs.title: Consumer financial law and contracts
what: Consumer financial products, such as loans, cards, bank accounts and investments, come with legal responsibilities on both sides. Providers must disclose costs clearly, treat customers fairly, protect their data and avoid unfair, deceptive or abusive acts and practices (UDAAP). Consumers are responsible for reading what they sign, paying as agreed, keeping records and reporting errors or fraud promptly, which protects their legal rights.

Every financial product is a contract. A legally binding contract needs an offer, acceptance, consideration (something of value exchanged), parties with capacity (generally adults of sound mind), a legal purpose and genuine agreement. Minors can usually cancel (void) contracts, which is one reason lenders require adult cosigners for under-18s. Breaking a contract gives the other side remedies such as damages or, for loans, repossession or collection.
how: Truth in Lending Act / Regulation Z: APR and finance charge disclosure, card rules, right to cancel some home loans within 3 days.
Truth in Savings Act / Regulation DD: banks must disclose APY and fees on deposit accounts.
Electronic Fund Transfer Act / Regulation E: debit card and transfer protections and error resolution.
Fair Credit Reporting Act, Equal Credit Opportunity Act, Fair Debt Collection Practices Act, CARD Act, Gramm-Leach-Bliley privacy notices.
Consumers can file complaints with the CFPB, the FTC or their state attorney general; firms must respond.
nums: The CFPB receives millions of consumer complaints a year, most about credit reporting (CFPB complaint database).
Federal law caps credit card fraud liability at $50, and Regulation E caps debit losses at $50 if reported within 2 business days.
real: Overdraft fees became a major enforcement and policy issue; many large banks, including Capital One and Citi, eliminated overdraft fees on consumer accounts in 2022-2024.
Courts have struck down contracts with minors or terms that were hidden or unconscionable, which is why clear disclosures matter.
traps: Consideration means each side gives something of value.
Truth in Lending is about credit; Truth in Savings is about deposit accounts.
subs.say: "Before you sign, let's read the three numbers that matter: the APR, the total finance charge and any penalty fees. The law requires the lender to show you all three."

qs.q: What responsibilities does our client have when using a financial product?
qs.a: Read the disclosures, pay on time, keep records and report problems fast. Lenders must show the APR and fees under the Truth in Lending Act, but the client has to actually read them. Reporting an unauthorized debit within two business days caps the loss at $50, and waiting can cost far more. Keeping statements and receipts means any dispute can be proven. Knowing their rights and duties protects them.

qs.q: What makes a contract legally binding?
qs.a: Six things: an offer, acceptance, consideration (something of value exchanged), parties with legal capacity, a legal purpose and genuine agreement without fraud or pressure. A car loan has all six: the lender offers money, you accept, you exchange payments for the car, you're an adult, buying a car is legal and the terms are disclosed. If a 16-year-old signs alone, they lack capacity, so lenders require an adult cosigner.

subs.title: Ethics in finance, accounting and financial information
what: Ethics is doing what's right when the law doesn't force you to, or when no one is watching. In finance, ethical duties include putting clients' interests first, disclosing conflicts of interest and fees, keeping information confidential, giving honest and fair advice, and never misleading anyone with numbers. A fiduciary must act in the client's best interest; brokers under Regulation Best Interest must act in the client's best interest when recommending, and disclose conflicts.

In accounting and financial-information management, ethics means integrity, objectivity and independence: reporting numbers accurately even when they're bad news, not 'managing' earnings to hit targets, protecting data, and resisting pressure from bosses. Ethical failures in finance are especially damaging because trust is the product. When it's lost, firms collapse, as Enron's auditor Arthur Andersen did in 2002.
how: Quick ethics test: Is it legal? Is it fair to everyone affected? Would I be comfortable seeing it in the news? What would a trusted mentor say?
Common conflicts: commissions that reward selling certain products, gifts from vendors, trading ahead of clients, recommending in-house funds.
Professional codes: CFP Board's fiduciary standard, the CFA Institute Code and Standards, the AICPA Code of Professional Conduct.
Whistleblowers who report securities fraud can receive 10%-30% of sanctions over $1 million through the SEC program, with legal protection from retaliation.
Data ethics: use customer data only for its stated purpose, get consent and protect it.
nums: The SEC whistleblower program has paid more than $2 billion in awards since 2011 (SEC).
Form CRS, required since 2020, makes brokers and advisers give clients a short plain-English summary of services, fees and conflicts (SEC).
real: Enron's collapse in 2001 erased about $74 billion of shareholder value and destroyed Arthur Andersen, one of the 'Big Five' accounting firms.
Wells Fargo employees opened millions of fake accounts to meet sales goals, a case study in how incentives can push good people to act unethically.
traps: Legal and ethical aren't the same; something can be legal and still unethical.
Disclosing a conflict doesn't remove it; you still must act in the client's interest.
subs.say: "We get paid a flat fee, not commissions, so we earn the same whichever fund we recommend. Our only incentive is your result."

qs.q: How would you handle a conflict of interest with this client?
qs.a: Disclose it clearly, then put the client first anyway. If our firm pays a higher commission on its own funds, we'd tell the client that up front, show a lower-cost alternative side by side and let the numbers decide. That's what Regulation Best Interest and the CFP fiduciary standard require. Better yet, a flat-fee structure removes the conflict entirely. Trust is the product we're selling.

qs.q: Your manager asks you to make this quarter's numbers look better. What do you do?
qs.a: Decline and explain why. Moving expenses or booking revenue early to hit a target is earnings manipulation, and it's how WorldCom and Enron started. I'd offer honest options instead, like explaining the miss with a clear recovery plan. If the pressure continued, I'd go to compliance or the audit committee, and the SEC whistleblower program protects people who report fraud. Short-term pressure is never worth the firm's integrity or my career.

subs.title: Legal considerations and technology in accounting
what: Accounting is governed by law as well as standards. Public companies must file financial statements with the SEC that follow GAAP and are audited by an independent CPA firm registered with the Public Company Accounting Oversight Board (PCAOB), created by Sarbanes-Oxley. Under SOX, the CEO and CFO personally certify the statements (Section 302), management must assess internal controls over financial reporting (Section 404), and knowingly certifying false statements can mean prison. Tax law, payroll law and record-retention rules apply to every business.

Technology has transformed accounting. Cloud software like QuickBooks Online and Xero links to bank accounts and categorizes transactions automatically; large companies run enterprise resource planning (ERP) systems like SAP and Oracle. Automation handles invoices and reconciliations, data analytics let auditors test every transaction instead of a sample, AI drafts reports and flags anomalies, and SEC filings are tagged in XBRL so computers can read them. The trade-off is cybersecurity and data-quality risk.
how: SOX 302: CEO/CFO certify reports. SOX 404: internal control assessment. SOX 802: penalties for destroying records. SOX 906: criminal penalties for false certification.
The SEC's clawback rule (effective 2023) requires listed companies to recover executive bonuses based on financial results that are later restated.
Records: the IRS generally requires keeping tax records for at least 3 years; employment tax records for 4 years.
Technology controls: user access limits, audit trails, backups, segregation of duties inside the software.
Blockchain can create shared, tamper-resistant ledgers, and auditors increasingly test crypto holdings.
nums: Sarbanes-Oxley was passed in 2002 after the Enron and WorldCom scandals (SEC).
SEC filings have used XBRL data tagging since 2009, making financial data machine-readable (SEC).
real: Wirecard, a German payments company, collapsed in 2020 after admitting that about 1.9 billion euros of cash on its balance sheet probably didn't exist; its auditor missed it for years.
Big accounting firms now use AI to analyze entire general ledgers for unusual entries during audits.
traps: The PCAOB oversees auditors of public companies; FASB sets accounting standards.
SOX applies mainly to public companies, but its practices are often adopted by private firms.
subs.say: "With cloud accounting connected to your bank, your books update daily, so you'll see a cash problem in days instead of finding it at tax time."

qs.q: What legal risks should a growing company watch in its accounting?
qs.a: Accuracy, tax compliance and records. If it plans to go public, Sarbanes-Oxley will require the CEO and CFO to certify the statements and the company to test its internal controls, so building those controls now is cheaper. Every business must file accurate tax and payroll returns and keep records at least three years. Misstated numbers can bring penalties, restated bonuses under the SEC clawback rule and lost trust. Clean books are a legal shield.

qs.q: How would you use technology to improve this business's accounting?
qs.a: Move to cloud accounting linked to the bank and payment apps, so transactions record automatically and the owner sees real-time reports. Automate invoicing and reminders to speed up cash collection. Add user permissions so the person entering bills can't approve them. That's segregation of duties built into the software. The time saved on data entry goes into analysis, like weekly cash forecasts.

title: Governance & the finance industry
blurb: Corporate governance, convergence and consolidation in the industry, and fintech and AI.

subs.title: Corporate governance
what: Corporate governance is the system of rules, practices and people that direct and control a company, balancing the interests of shareholders, managers, employees, customers, lenders and the community. Shareholders elect a board of directors, the board hires and oversees the CEO and sets strategy and risk appetite, and managers run daily operations. Good governance keeps managers accountable, decisions transparent and the company's long-term health ahead of short-term pressure.

A well-governed company has an independent board with relevant expertise, key committees (audit, compensation, nominating and governance, often risk), a clear code of conduct, transparent and timely reporting, strong internal and external audit, and fair treatment of shareholders. Governance structures depend on ownership (public, private, family or founder-controlled), size, industry regulation, laws and stock exchange rules, culture and pressure from investors. Every employee has a role: following the code, keeping accurate records and speaking up about problems.
how: NYSE and Nasdaq require a majority of independent directors and fully independent audit committees.
Separating the CEO and board chair roles, or naming a lead independent director, adds oversight.
Dual-class shares (Meta, Alphabet) give founders voting control with a minority of the equity, a governance trade-off.
Governance shapes decisions: big moves need board approval, which slows decisions but improves them, and risk committees review major bets.
Employee's role: follow policies, report concerns through hotlines, avoid conflicts of interest, and keep records honest.
nums: About 85% of S&P 500 directors are independent (Spencer Stuart U.S. Board Index).
Sarbanes-Oxley requires audit committees of listed companies to be made up entirely of independent directors (SEC).
real: In November 2023 OpenAI's nonprofit board fired CEO Sam Altman, then reinstated him within days after employees and investors revolted, a case study in how governance structure shapes control.
WeWork's 2019 IPO collapsed after filings revealed weak governance, including founder control and conflicts of interest; its valuation fell from $47 billion to under $10 billion.
traps: The board oversees; management manages.
Independent directors have no material ties to the company or its managers.
subs.say: "Good governance means someone independent is checking the decisions. For your family business, an advisory board with two outside members would add that discipline."

qs.q: Why does corporate governance matter to investors and clients?
qs.a: Because it decides whether the people running the company are held accountable. An independent board, honest reporting and a strong audit committee make fraud and reckless bets less likely. Investors pay more for well-governed companies. WeWork's valuation fell from $47 billion to under $10 billion when weak governance came out before its IPO. For our client, good governance means their investment is protected by more than the CEO's word.

qs.q: What can an ordinary employee do to support good governance?
qs.a: Follow the code of conduct, keep records accurate and speak up. Most fraud is caught by tips, so an employee who reports a problem through the hotline is part of governance. Employees should also disclose conflicts of interest, like a vendor who's a relative, and never cut corners to hit a target. When everyone does that, the board's oversight actually works.

subs.title: Convergence and consolidation in the finance industry
what: Convergence is the blurring of lines between types of financial firms: banks sell insurance and investments, insurers offer savings products, brokerages offer checking accounts and tech companies offer payments and loans. The Gramm-Leach-Bliley Act of 1999 made this legal by repealing parts of Glass-Steagall, right after the 1998 Citicorp-Travelers merger created Citigroup, a 'financial supermarket.' Today, fintechs and big tech firms are converging into finance too.

Consolidation is the shrinking number of firms through mergers and acquisitions. The U.S. had more than 17,000 FDIC-insured institutions in 1984 and 4,238 in mid-2026. Drivers include economies of scale (spreading technology and compliance costs over more customers), geographic reach, diversification, deposits for funding and rescues of failing banks. Benefits include efficiency and broader services; costs include less competition, fewer local banks, job losses and 'too big to fail' risk.
how: Horizontal merger: two firms in the same business (two banks). Conglomerate or cross-industry: a bank buying an insurer.
Benefits to customers: one-stop shopping, bigger ATM networks, better technology. Risks: higher fees, less personal service, branch closures.
Regulators (Fed, OCC, FDIC, Department of Justice) review bank mergers for competition and safety.
Systemically important banks face stricter capital rules and annual stress tests.
Community banks compete through relationships, local decision-making and niche lending.
nums: FDIC-insured institutions fell to 4,238 in the second quarter of 2026; 36 merged with other banks in that quarter alone (FDIC).
Capital One completed its roughly $35 billion acquisition of Discover in May 2025, combining a card issuer with a payment network.
real: JPMorgan Chase bought First Republic Bank in May 2023 after it failed, making the largest U.S. bank even larger.
In 2023 UBS took over Credit Suisse in a Swiss government-brokered rescue, merging two of Europe's biggest banks.
traps: Convergence = firms offering each other's products; consolidation = fewer, bigger firms.
Gramm-Leach-Bliley (1999) enabled convergence; it didn't create the FDIC.
subs.say: "Because of consolidation, the number of U.S. banks has fallen by about three-quarters since 1984. A local credit union can still give you the personal service big banks are losing."

qs.q: How does consolidation in banking affect our client?
qs.a: There are pros and cons. Bigger banks offer better apps, more ATMs and more products under one roof, like Capital One adding the Discover network in 2025. But fewer competitors can mean higher fees, branch closures and less personal service, especially for small businesses that need a banker who knows them. We'd compare the big bank's convenience with a community bank or credit union's service, and pick based on what the client needs most.

qs.q: Why do banks merge?
qs.a: Mainly for scale. Technology, cybersecurity and compliance costs are huge, and spreading them over more customers lowers the cost per account. Mergers also add deposits, new regions and new products, and sometimes rescue a failing bank, as when JPMorgan bought First Republic in 2023. The number of insured institutions fell from more than 17,000 in 1984 to 4,238 by mid-2026, and 36 merged in one recent quarter alone.

subs.title: Fintech, AI and technology in financial services
what: Fintech is technology that delivers financial services in new ways: mobile banking, peer-to-peer payments (Venmo, Zelle), robo-advisors (Betterment, Wealthfront, Schwab Intelligent Portfolios), buy now, pay later, neobanks (Chime), online lenders, crypto exchanges and stablecoins. It has lowered costs, made accounts cheaper to open and brought services to people traditional banks underserved. Most fintechs partner with chartered banks, so regulation and FDIC coverage still flow through the bank.

Artificial intelligence is now built into finance: fraud detection that scores each card swipe in milliseconds, chatbots and virtual assistants, credit underwriting with more data, trading algorithms, compliance monitoring and drafting reports. The risks are real: biased models that discriminate, privacy breaches, errors or 'hallucinations', and models no one can explain. Fair-lending law still requires lenders to give specific reasons when they deny credit, even if an AI made the decision.
how: Robo-advisors build and rebalance diversified portfolios automatically for fees often around 0.25% a year or less.
Banks' AI fraud tools analyze location, device, amount and habits to flag unusual activity in real time.
Model risk management: test AI models for accuracy and bias, document them, monitor them and keep humans in the loop.
The GENIUS Act (July 2025) set federal rules for payment stablecoins, including full reserves in cash or short-term Treasuries.
Cybersecurity is the flip side: more digital services mean more attack surface.
nums: Bank of America's virtual assistant Erica has handled billions of client interactions since its 2018 launch (Bank of America).
The SEC approved the first spot bitcoin ETFs in January 2024, bringing crypto into regulated brokerage accounts (SEC).
real: The 2024 Synapse collapse showed fintech's middleman risk: when a banking-as-a-service provider failed, customers of several apps lost access to their funds for months.
JPMorgan Chase says it spends more than $15 billion a year on technology, part of why big banks are investing heavily in AI.
traps: A fintech app usually isn't a bank; FDIC coverage depends on its partner bank.
AI decisions in lending still must follow fair-lending laws.
subs.say: "A robo-advisor can automate your investing for about 0.25% a year, while we focus on the human parts: your goals, your fears and the big decisions."

qs.q: Why should our client pay for a human advisor when robo-advisors are so cheap?
qs.a: For simple investing, a robo-advisor at about 0.25% a year is excellent, and we'd say so. A human adds value where judgment and emotion matter: coordinating taxes, insurance, estate planning and big life decisions, and keeping the client from panic-selling in a crash. Studies by firms like Vanguard estimate that behavioral coaching alone can add meaningful value. Many clients use both: a robo-advisor for the portfolio and an advisor for the plan.

qs.q: What are the risks of banks using AI?
qs.a: Bias, errors, privacy and accountability. An AI trained on biased data could deny loans unfairly, which is illegal under fair-lending laws, and lenders must still explain every denial. Models can make confident mistakes, and they rely on sensitive personal data. Good practice is testing models for bias, keeping humans in the loop for big decisions and strong cybersecurity. Used that way, AI catches fraud faster while customers stay protected.

title: Client service & careers
blurb: A finance professional's responsibilities to clients, CRM technology, handling difficult situations, and careers and networking in finance.

subs.title: Responsibilities of finance professionals to clients
what: Finance professionals hold clients' money and futures in their hands, so the job comes with clear responsibilities. First, know the client: their goals, timeline, income, assets, debts, risk tolerance and family situation. Second, act in their best interest and recommend only what fits. Third, communicate clearly: explain options, risks and costs in plain language, without jargon. Fourth, protect their information and keep it confidential. Fifth, follow through, with timely service, documented decisions and regular reviews.

Legal standards back these duties up. Registered investment advisers and CFP professionals are fiduciaries. Brokers must follow Regulation Best Interest. Every firm must give clients Form CRS, a short summary of services, fees and conflicts. Professionals must also watch for signs of elder financial abuse and may add a 'trusted contact' to accounts, which FINRA Rule 4512 encourages. Great client service goes beyond the rules: it's being the person the client trusts when things go wrong.
how: Discovery meeting: ask open questions ('What would financial security look like for you?'), listen more than talk, and summarize back.
Suitability and best interest: match products to the client's profile, and document why.
Disclose fees and conflicts up front, in dollars, not just percentages.
Confidentiality: Gramm-Leach-Bliley privacy rules; never discuss a client's affairs without permission.
Ongoing duty: annual reviews, updates after life events, prompt answers, and education so clients understand their plan.
The Senior Safe Act (2018) protects trained employees who report suspected elder financial exploitation in good faith.
nums: Form CRS has been required for brokers and investment advisers since June 30, 2020 (SEC).
People 60 and older reported about $3 billion in fraud losses to the FTC in 2025 (FTC), which is why trusted-contact forms matter.
real: The 2026 FTDM district case asked advisors to explain the responsibilities of finance professionals to nervous new parents, a sign of how central this PI is.
Many firms now hold 'family meetings' that include adult children, with the client's permission, to plan for aging and reduce exploitation risk.
traps: A fiduciary standard is stricter than a suitability standard.
Confidentiality has limits: suspected fraud and legal orders can require disclosure.
subs.say: "Our responsibility is simple: understand your goals, recommend only what's in your best interest, explain every cost in dollars and check in with you at least once a year."

qs.q: What are your responsibilities to us as our financial advisor?
qs.a: Four promises. We'll get to know your goals and situation before recommending anything. We'll act in your best interest, as fiduciaries, and disclose every fee and conflict in plain dollars. We'll keep your information confidential and secure. And we'll stay with you: an annual review and a call after any big life event, like a new baby or job change. You can verify our record on FINRA BrokerCheck anytime.

qs.q: How would you earn the trust of a client who has been burned before?
qs.a: Listen first, then make everything transparent. We'd ask what went wrong last time and promise not to repeat it. Show every fee in dollars, explain recommendations in plain language and put the plan in writing. Start with small, low-risk steps, like building an emergency fund, so they see results before bigger decisions. Then follow through on every promise, on time. Trust is rebuilt by consistency, not by a pitch.

subs.title: Customer relationship management (CRM) and technology
what: Customer relationship management is the strategy of building long-term, profitable relationships with clients by understanding and serving them better than competitors. CRM technology, software like Salesforce Financial Services Cloud, Wealthbox or Redtail for advisors, stores every client's profile, accounts, goals, documents, meeting notes and interactions in one place, so anyone on the team can give informed, personal service.

CRM systems also automate work: reminders for annual reviews and birthdays, tasks after a meeting, segmenting clients by needs, tracking referrals and measuring satisfaction. Analytics can flag clients who might leave or who would benefit from a new service. Ethics matter: client data must be collected with consent, used only for its purpose, kept secure and never used to push products clients don't need.
how: Track: contact details, family members, goals, risk profile, accounts, meeting notes, preferences (text vs call), life events.
Automate: review reminders, follow-up emails, document requests, compliance logs of client communications.
Segment: by life stage (new parents, pre-retirees), by service level, by product need.
Measure: retention rate, referrals, Net Promoter Score, response time.
Ethics and law: privacy notices, data security, consent for marketing, no misleading personalization.

Advanced database use: a CRM is a relational database; queries, filters and reports pull lists such as 'clients over 60 with no trusted contact' or 'families whose child turns 18 this year', and dashboards join account data with interaction history.
nums: Bain & Company research found that raising customer retention by 5% can raise profits by 25% to 95%, a classic case for CRM.
Salesforce is among the most widely used CRM platforms, and its Financial Services Cloud is built for banks, advisors and insurers.
real: USAA is known for top customer-satisfaction scores, partly because its systems give every representative a full view of the member's accounts and history.
Advisors who log life events in CRM can reach out proactively, for example reviewing insurance when a client's child turns 16 and starts driving.
traps: CRM is a strategy supported by technology, not just software.
Retention is usually cheaper than winning new customers.
subs.say: "We'd log your goals and key dates in our CRM, so we'll reach out before your daughter starts college, not after the bills arrive."

qs.q: How would you use technology to keep this client relationship strong?
qs.a: With a CRM that remembers everything and prompts action. We'd record their goals, family, preferences and every conversation, then set automatic reminders for annual reviews and key life events, like a child's 16th birthday for car insurance or college deadlines. The system would flag if they haven't heard from us in 90 days. That turns a once-a-year relationship into proactive service, which is what keeps clients and earns referrals.

qs.q: What ethical issues come with collecting so much client data?
qs.a: Privacy, security and purpose. We'd collect only what's needed to serve the client, explain how it's used in our privacy notice, protect it with encryption and access limits, and never sell it or use it to push products they don't need. Under Gramm-Leach-Bliley, financial firms must give privacy notices and safeguard data. A breach or misuse would destroy the trust the CRM is supposed to build.

subs.title: Handling difficult clients, complaints and cultural differences
what: Difficult moments in finance usually come from fear or frustration: a market drop, a denied loan, a fee they didn't expect, a mistake by the firm. The goal is to calm the situation, solve the real problem and keep the relationship. A simple model is LAST: Listen fully without interrupting, Apologize for the experience (even if it isn't your fault), Solve the problem or explain the next steps, and Thank them for raising it. Staying calm, using their name and not taking anger personally are essential.

Clients also differ by culture, language, age, financial experience and beliefs about money. Some cultures avoid debt or interest; some families make money decisions together; some clients prefer formal communication. Adapting means asking about preferences instead of assuming, avoiding jargon and idioms, using translated materials or interpreters, respecting family roles and checking understanding. That's good service and, under fair-lending and fair-treatment rules, a legal duty too.
how: Complaint steps: listen, acknowledge, apologize, investigate, solve or escalate, follow up, document.
Never argue, blame the client or make promises you can't keep; offer choices.
Escalate when needed: a supervisor, compliance (if it involves a possible rule violation) or the formal complaint process.
Market-panic calls: acknowledge the fear, remind them of the plan and their timeline, show history, and agree on a next step.

Cultural adaptation: plain language, interpreter services, materials in the client's language, flexible meeting formats, awareness of religious finance needs (e.g. interest-free Islamic finance products).
nums: Companies must respond to complaints filed through the CFPB portal, generally within 15 days (CFPB).
About 1 in 5 U.S. residents speaks a language other than English at home (U.S. Census Bureau).
real: During the March 2020 crash, advisors who called clients first, before clients called them, kept far more clients from selling at the bottom.
Some banks and credit unions now offer Sharia-compliant home financing for Muslim customers who avoid paying interest.
traps: Apologizing for the experience isn't admitting legal fault.
Adapting to culture means asking, not stereotyping.
subs.say: "I completely understand why seeing that drop is scary. Let's look at your plan together: this money isn't needed for 20 years, and every past drop like this has recovered."

qs.q: The market just fell 15% and our client wants to sell everything. What do you say?
qs.a: First acknowledge the fear: 'It's completely normal to feel this way.' Then remind them of their plan: this money is for retirement in 25 years, and their emergency fund covers short-term needs. Show history: the S&P 500 fell about 37% in 2008 and 18% in 2022 and recovered both times, while people who sold locked in losses. Offer a concrete step, like rebalancing or keeping their monthly investments going at lower prices. Calm, specific and empathetic keeps them on track.

qs.q: A client is angry about a fee they didn't expect. How do you handle it?
qs.a: Listen fully, apologize for the surprise and investigate right away. If the fee was our mistake or poorly explained, reverse it and fix the disclosure. If it was correct, explain clearly what it's for and show ways to avoid it, like setting up a minimum balance or autopay. Then follow up in writing and log it in the CRM so it doesn't happen again. A complaint handled well often makes a client more loyal than one who never had a problem.

qs.q: How would you adapt your advice for a client from a different cultural background?
qs.a: Ask about their preferences instead of assuming. Some clients want family members in the meeting, some prefer materials in another language, and some avoid interest for religious reasons, so we'd offer options like interest-free financing where available. We'd use plain language, check understanding often and respect how they make decisions. Good advice only works if the client trusts and understands it.

subs.title: Careers and professional relationships in finance
what: Finance offers careers in five big areas. Banking: tellers, personal bankers, loan officers, branch managers, commercial lenders. Investments: financial advisors and planners, research analysts, portfolio managers, traders, investment bankers. Insurance: agents, underwriters, claims adjusters, actuaries. Accounting: staff accountants, auditors, tax professionals, forensic accountants. Corporate finance: financial analysts, treasury, FP&A, controllers and CFOs. Growing fields include fintech, compliance, risk management, data analytics and cybersecurity.

Professional relationships drive finance careers because the industry runs on trust and referrals. Ways to build them: internships, DECA and other student organizations, informational interviews, LinkedIn, professional associations (the Financial Planning Association, CFA societies, state CPA societies), mentors and alumni networks. Licenses and credentials signal skill and ethics: the SIE exam is open to anyone 18 or older, then Series 7 and 66 for brokers and advisors, state insurance licenses, and the CPA, CFP and CFA designations.
how: Entry paths: business, finance, accounting or economics degrees; many banks hire high-school graduates as tellers with tuition help.
Key skills: analysis, communication, ethics, Excel and data tools, relationship building, staying calm under pressure.
Credentials: CFP (planning, fiduciary), CFA (investment analysis), CPA (accounting, licensed by states), FRM (risk), insurance licenses.
Networking: give before you ask, follow up within 24 hours, keep in touch, and thank people who help.
Professional image: online presence, handshake and eye contact, punctuality, clear writing.
nums: Personal financial advisors and financial analysts earned median pay of about $100,000 in 2024, and accountants about $80,000 (BLS Occupational Outlook Handbook).
The SIE (Securities Industry Essentials) exam can be taken at 18 without sponsorship from a firm (FINRA).
real: Many top banks, including JPMorgan Chase and Goldman Sachs, recruit summer interns heavily from the year before graduation and make many full-time offers from those programs.
Bank of America and others run programs that hire high-school graduates and pay for further education.
traps: The CPA is a state license; the CFP and CFA are professional certifications.
Networking is building relationships over time, not just asking for jobs.
subs.say: "As DECA members, we've learned that finance runs on relationships: we'd connect you with a CPA for taxes and an estate attorney, and coordinate everyone on one plan."

qs.q: What career in finance interests you, and why?
qs.a: Financial planning, because it combines analysis with helping real people. Preparing for this event showed us how a plan for a family, like an emergency fund, the right insurance and automatic investing, changes their future. Planners earn a median of about $100,000, and the CFP fiduciary standard fits how we want to work. We'd start by passing the SIE, then intern with a planning firm. It's a career where trust is the product.

qs.q: How would you build professional relationships in the finance industry?
qs.a: Start early and give value first. DECA, internships and informational interviews with alumni let us meet professionals now. We'd follow up within a day, thank people and stay in touch with useful updates, not just requests. Joining groups like the Financial Planning Association's student chapters builds a network that leads to referrals and mentors. In finance, your network is often how clients and opportunities find you.

title: Fraud & identity protection
blurb: Protecting against identity theft, recognizing and stopping scams, and preventing fraud inside a business.

subs.title: Protecting against identity theft and securing online accounts
what: Identity theft is when someone uses your personal information, such as a Social Security number, account number, login or medical ID, to open accounts, make purchases, file tax returns or get medical care in your name. It can take months to discover and years to clean up. Children are targets too, because their clean credit files often go unchecked until they apply for a first loan. Synthetic identity fraud mixes real and fake details to create a new 'person.'

Prevention is a layered habit. Freeze credit at all three bureaus (free, and you can unfreeze in minutes when applying for credit). Use a password manager with unique passwords and app-based multifactor authentication. Turn on account alerts, review statements weekly, shred documents, limit what you share on social media and avoid banking on public Wi-Fi. Get an IRS Identity Protection PIN to block fraudulent tax filings. If it happens, act fast with a recovery plan from IdentityTheft.gov.
how: Credit freeze: free at Equifax, Experian and TransUnion; blocks new accounts; doesn't affect your score.
Fraud alert: lasts one year (seven for confirmed victims); lenders must verify your identity.
MFA: an authenticator app or passkey beats a texted code, which can be stolen by SIM-swap attacks.
IRS IP PIN: a six-digit number, available to anyone who verifies their identity, that's required to file a return in your name.
If victimized: report at IdentityTheft.gov, freeze credit, change passwords, contact affected companies, file a police report if needed, and check credit reports.
nums: The FTC received more than a million identity theft reports in 2024 (FTC Consumer Sentinel Network).
The 2017 Equifax breach exposed personal data on about 147 million Americans (FTC).
real: In 2024 a breach at National Public Data exposed records including Social Security numbers for a huge number of people, another reason experts recommend freezing credit by default.
SIM-swap criminals have stolen millions in crypto by taking over victims' phone numbers and intercepting text codes.
traps: A freeze stops new accounts; it doesn't stop misuse of existing cards.
Checking your own credit never hurts your score.
subs.say: "Three steps today: freeze your credit at all three bureaus, turn on app-based two-factor login for your bank and email, and set alerts for every transaction."

qs.q: What's the single best thing our client can do to protect their identity?
qs.a: Freeze their credit at Equifax, Experian and TransUnion. It's free, takes about 15 minutes online and stops criminals from opening new accounts in their name, and they can lift it in minutes when they apply for credit. After that, a password manager and app-based two-factor login on the bank and email accounts. The Equifax breach exposed 147 million people, so we assume data is already out there and lock the doors.

qs.q: Our client's identity was just stolen. What should they do first?
qs.a: Act today. Go to IdentityTheft.gov for an FTC recovery plan and report, freeze credit at all three bureaus, and call the fraud departments of any affected accounts to close or flag them. Change passwords, starting with email, since it resets everything else. Then pull all three free credit reports and dispute anything fraudulent. An IRS IP PIN prevents tax-refund fraud next season. Moving fast limits the damage and their liability.

subs.title: Recognizing and stopping scams
what: Scams trick people into handing over money or information themselves, which makes them harder to reverse than theft. The biggest categories today are investment scams (often crypto 'opportunities' that start on social media or dating apps, sometimes called 'pig butchering'), impostor scams (fake bank fraud departments, government agencies, tech support or a relative in trouble), romance scams, fake job offers, phishing texts and emails, and fake-check scams. AI now lets criminals clone voices and create convincing fake videos.

Nearly every scam shares the same red flags: urgency ('act now'), secrecy ('don't tell your bank'), an unusual payment method (gift cards, crypto, wire transfers, payment apps, cash couriers), an unsolicited contact and a promise that's too good to be true. The best defense is a pause: hang up, look up the official number yourself and call back. Banks never ask you to move money to 'protect' it or to read them a one-time code.
how: Never pay with gift cards, crypto or wire transfers to someone who contacted you first.
Verify independently: call the number on the back of your card or the official website, never the number in the message.
Family code word: a phrase that proves a caller claiming to be a relative is real (defends against AI voice clones).
Report scams to ReportFraud.ftc.gov, and internet crimes to the FBI's IC3.gov; call your bank immediately to try to stop payments.
Older clients: add a trusted contact to accounts, and talk openly with family about common scams.
nums: Americans reported a record $15.9 billion in fraud losses to the FTC in 2025, up about 25% from 2024; investment scams were about $7.9 billion, nearly half (FTC).
Impostor scams were the most-reported type, with about $3.5 billion lost in 2025 (FTC).
The FBI's Internet Crime Complaint Center counted about $20.9 billion in reported losses for 2025 (FBI IC3).
real: Pig-butchering scammers build relationships for weeks over text or dating apps, then steer victims to fake crypto trading sites that show phony gains until the victim tries to withdraw.
In a widely reported 2024 case, an employee at the engineering firm Arup in Hong Kong sent about $25 million after a video call with deepfakes of company executives.
traps: Your bank will never ask for a one-time passcode.
Payment-app transfers you authorize are hard to reverse, even if you were tricked.
subs.say: "If anyone pressures you to pay right now with gift cards, crypto or a wire, it's a scam. Hang up and call us or your bank at the number you already know."

qs.q: How would you protect an older client from scams?
qs.a: With a mix of education and safeguards. We'd add a trusted contact to their accounts, which FINRA rules encourage, so we can call someone if something looks wrong. We'd set alerts and transfer limits, and agree on a family code word to defeat AI voice-clone calls. And we'd teach the three red flags: urgency, secrecy and unusual payment methods like gift cards or crypto. People 60 and older reported about $3 billion in losses in 2025, so this is real protection.

qs.q: A client says someone from their bank called asking them to move money to a 'safe account.' What do you tell them?
qs.a: That it's a scam, and to stop right now. Real banks never ask you to move money to protect it or to share a one-time code. Hang up and call the number on the back of the card. If any money has been sent, call the bank's fraud line immediately to try to stop it, then report it at ReportFraud.ftc.gov. Impostor scams cost Americans about $3.5 billion in 2025, and the pause before acting is the best defense.

subs.title: Fraud inside businesses (occupational fraud)
what: Occupational fraud is when employees, managers or executives misuse their position to steal from their own organization. The Association of Certified Fraud Examiners groups it into three types: asset misappropriation (stealing cash, inventory or using company cards for personal spending), the most common; corruption (bribes, kickbacks, conflicts of interest); and financial statement fraud (falsifying results), the least common but the costliest.

The fraud triangle explains why it happens: pressure (debt, addiction, unrealistic targets), opportunity (weak controls) and rationalization ('I'll pay it back', 'they underpay me'). Businesses can't remove pressure, but they can remove opportunity with controls and reduce rationalization with a strong ethical culture. Most frauds are caught by tips from employees, customers or vendors, so a hotline is one of the most effective controls.
how: Controls: segregation of duties, dual approval, bank reconciliations by someone independent, surprise audits, mandatory vacations, job rotation, inventory counts.
Tip hotline: anonymous, available to employees, vendors and customers.
Red flags: living beyond means, refusing vacations, unusually close vendor relationships, control-override attempts.
Data analytics: test 100% of transactions for duplicates, round numbers, weekend entries and Benford's Law anomalies.
Fidelity bonds or crime insurance transfer some of the loss.
nums: Organizations lose an estimated 5% of revenue to fraud each year; the median loss per case was $145,000 (ACFE 2024 Report to the Nations).
Tips detected 43% of frauds, more than any other method, and the typical fraud lasted 12 months before discovery (ACFE 2024).
Financial statement fraud was the costliest type, with a median loss of $766,000 (ACFE 2024).
real: Small businesses with few employees are hit hard because one bookkeeper often handles everything; ACFE data shows small organizations suffer large median losses relative to their size.
Rita Crundwell, comptroller of Dixon, Illinois, stole about $53 million over two decades by controlling a secret bank account; she was caught when a coworker covering for her vacation noticed it.
traps: Asset misappropriation is the most common; financial statement fraud is the most expensive.
Tips, not audits, catch the most fraud.
subs.say: "Most fraud is caught by tips, so we'd set up an anonymous hotline and make sure the person who writes the checks never reconciles the bank account."

qs.q: How would you protect this small business from employee theft?
qs.a: Remove the opportunity. Split duties so the person who pays bills doesn't reconcile the bank account; the owner can review the reconciliation monthly. Require two approvals for payments over a set amount, run surprise cash counts and make everyone take vacation, which is how the $53 million Dixon, Illinois, theft was finally caught. Add an anonymous tip line, since tips catch 43% of frauds. These controls cost little next to the median $145,000 loss.

qs.q: Why do trusted employees commit fraud?
qs.a: The fraud triangle: pressure, opportunity and rationalization. A loyal employee facing big medical bills, with sole control of the books, might tell themselves they'll 'borrow' and repay. The business can't remove the pressure, but it can remove the opportunity with controls and reduce rationalization with a culture where ethics are discussed and help, like an employee assistance program, is available. Good people stay good when the system supports them.

title: Starting & running a business
blurb: Types of business ownership, entrepreneurship and the owner's role, and what drives profit and business risk.

subs.title: Types of business ownership
what: The form of ownership decides who controls the business, who is liable for its debts, how it's taxed and how it can raise money. A sole proprietorship is one owner, easy and cheap to start, but the owner has unlimited personal liability. A partnership has two or more owners sharing profits, control and, in a general partnership, unlimited liability; limited partnerships and LLPs limit some partners' liability. A partnership agreement is essential.

A corporation is a separate legal entity owned by shareholders, with limited liability and the ability to sell stock, but more paperwork. A C corporation pays corporate tax and shareholders pay tax again on dividends; an S corporation passes income to owners to avoid double taxation but is limited to 100 shareholders and one class of stock. A limited liability company (LLC) combines limited liability with flexible pass-through taxation and is the most popular choice for small businesses today. Other forms include cooperatives, nonprofits and franchises.
how: Compare on five factors: liability, taxes, control, ability to raise money, continuity (does it survive the owner?).
Sole proprietorship: simplest; profits on the owner's return (Schedule C); unlimited liability.
General partnership: shared management and unlimited, joint liability; ends if a partner leaves unless the agreement says otherwise.
C corp: unlimited growth through stock, double taxation, survives owners. S corp: pass-through, ownership limits.
LLC: limited liability, pass-through by default, flexible management; can elect S corp taxation.
Franchise: buy rights to a proven brand and system (fees and royalties, less independence).
nums: Sole proprietorships make up the majority of U.S. business tax returns, though corporations earn most business revenue (IRS Statistics of Income).
An S corporation can have no more than 100 shareholders and only one class of stock (IRS).
real: Apple began in 1976 as a partnership of Steve Jobs, Steve Wozniak and Ronald Wayne; Wayne sold his 10% stake for $800 within two weeks.
Ben & Jerry's started as a partnership in a converted Vermont gas station in 1978 and later became a corporation to raise money for growth.
traps: An LLC is not a corporation, though both offer limited liability.
Limited liability protects personal assets but not against personal guarantees or fraud.
subs.say: "Since you and your friend are starting together, we'd form an LLC with a written operating agreement. It protects your personal savings and spells out what happens if one of you leaves."

qs.q: What type of business ownership would you recommend for our client, and why?
qs.a: An LLC, for most small businesses starting out. It protects the owners' personal assets from business debts and lawsuits, profits pass through to their personal returns so there's no double taxation, and the paperwork is light. If profits grow, the LLC can elect S corporation taxation to save on self-employment tax. With a partner, a written operating agreement covering ownership splits, decisions and buyouts is essential. That gives protection now and flexibility later.

qs.q: Our client wants to go into business with a friend. What should they think about?
qs.a: Put everything in writing first. A partnership or LLC operating agreement should cover how much each person invests, how profits are split, who makes which decisions, what happens if someone wants out, and how disputes get resolved. In a general partnership, each partner can be personally liable for the other's business debts, which is why we'd recommend an LLC. Friendships survive businesses when expectations are clear from day one.

subs.title: Entrepreneurship and the role of the owner
what: Entrepreneurship is recognizing an opportunity and organizing resources to pursue it, accepting risk in exchange for potential reward. Entrepreneurs range from 'lifestyle' small-business owners (a bakery, a landscaping company) to scalable startups aiming for rapid growth, social entrepreneurs who build businesses to solve social problems, and intrapreneurs who innovate inside existing companies. Small businesses create a large share of new jobs and drive competition and innovation in a market economy.

The owner wears many hats, especially early on: visionary, salesperson, financial manager, hiring manager, compliance officer and risk manager. Key responsibilities include writing a business plan, securing funding, managing cash, meeting legal and tax obligations, hiring and leading people, and building customer relationships. Ethics in entrepreneurship, like honest marketing, fair treatment of employees and paying suppliers on time, builds the reputation small businesses depend on.
how: Common entrepreneur traits: initiative, resilience, comfort with risk, creativity, persistence, willingness to learn.
A business plan covers: executive summary, product or service, market analysis, competition, marketing, operations, management, financial projections and funding needs.
Validate before investing heavily: test with a small launch, pre-orders or a pop-up.
Free help: SBA, Small Business Development Centers (SBDCs) and SCORE mentors.
Ethics: honest claims, fair pay, data privacy, paying taxes and suppliers on time.
nums: Americans have filed more than 5 million new business applications each year since 2021, well above pre-pandemic levels (U.S. Census Bureau Business Formation Statistics).
Small businesses account for about 99.9% of U.S. businesses and employ nearly half of private-sector workers (SBA Office of Advocacy).
real: Airbnb's founders started by renting air mattresses in their apartment during a 2007 design conference, a small test that validated a huge idea.
TOMS Shoes popularized a 'one for one' social-entrepreneurship model, then later changed it as the company learned what helped communities most.
traps: Entrepreneurs accept risk; that's what distinguishes them from managers.
A business plan is for the owner's thinking as much as for lenders.
subs.say: "Before you spend $50,000 on a storefront, let's test the idea with a $2,000 pop-up for three weekends. If customers buy, we'll have real numbers for the bank."

qs.q: What's the biggest risk for this new business, and how do you reduce it?
qs.a: Running out of cash before the business proves itself. We'd reduce it three ways: test the idea cheaply first, with a pop-up or pre-orders, so the launch is based on real demand; keep startup costs lean by leasing equipment instead of buying it; and hold at least three to six months of expenses in reserve or an approved line of credit. We'd track cash weekly and set a clear point to change course if sales lag.

qs.q: What makes a successful entrepreneur?
qs.a: Persistence, learning fast and managing money well. Most successful founders test ideas before betting everything, like Airbnb's founders renting air mattresses first, then adjust quickly based on what customers do. They know their numbers, especially cash flow and break-even, and they build trust through ethical, reliable service. Free mentoring from SCORE or a Small Business Development Center helps first-timers avoid common mistakes.

subs.title: What drives business profit and business risk
what: Profit is what's left after a business pays all its expenses: revenue minus costs. It rewards owners for taking risk and signals that a business is creating value customers will pay for. Profit depends on price (what customers will pay), sales volume (demand), costs (fixed and variable), efficiency and productivity, competition, and the wider environment: the economy, interest rates, taxes and regulation.

Business risk is the chance that results fall short of expectations, or that the business fails. Sources include economic risk (recessions, inflation, interest rates), market and competitive risk (new rivals, changing tastes), operational risk (supply chain breakdowns, equipment failure), technological risk (disruption, cyberattacks), legal and regulatory risk, financial risk (too much debt), natural risk (disasters) and human risk (key-person loss, fraud, errors). Higher potential profit usually comes with higher risk.
how: Profit levers: raise price, sell more, cut variable costs, cut fixed costs, improve the product mix.
Profit margin = profit / revenue; a 1-point margin gain on $1 million of sales is $10,000.
Operating leverage: businesses with high fixed costs see profit swing more with sales.
Financial leverage: debt boosts returns in good times and losses in bad times.
Reduce risk by diversifying customers and suppliers, keeping cash reserves, insuring, using contracts and monitoring indicators.
nums: The average U.S. grocery store runs on a net profit margin of only about 1% to 3%, so small cost changes matter a lot (industry estimates).
Interest-rate changes affect profit directly through borrowing costs: with the Fed at 3.75%-4.00% and prime at 7.00% (Oct. 2026), variable-rate business loans cost more than in 2021.
real: Blockbuster's dominance disappeared after it passed on buying Netflix in 2000 and was slow to move to streaming, a case of technological and competitive risk.
COVID-era supply chain disruptions in 2021-22 pushed many companies to keep more inventory and add second suppliers, trading some profit for less risk.
traps: Profit isn't the same as revenue.
Higher risk doesn't guarantee higher profit; it only makes higher profit possible.
subs.say: "A 5% price increase on your best seller adds about $9,000 of profit a year without selling one more unit, the fastest profit lever you have."

qs.q: How could our client increase profit without increasing sales?
qs.a: Work on price and costs. A small price increase on items where customers are loyal goes straight to profit: 5% on $180,000 of sales is $9,000. Then cut variable costs, by renegotiating supplier prices, reducing waste and adjusting portions or packaging. Finally, shift effort toward the highest-margin products. We'd test the price change on one product first and track the margin monthly.

qs.q: What external factors could hurt this business, and how would you prepare?
qs.a: The economy, interest rates, competition and regulation. A recession would cut customer spending, so we'd keep three to six months of cash reserves. Higher rates raise borrowing costs, so we'd prefer fixed-rate financing. A new competitor could undercut prices, so we'd build loyalty through service. And we'd watch indicators like consumer spending and the jobs report monthly. Planning for the risks we can name makes the business resilient to the ones we can't.
